prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that periodically reads moisture levels from a DFRobot Soil Moisture Sensor v2.0, an analog resistive sensor, via an MCP3008 analog-to-digital converter connected over the SPI bus. Wire the MCP3008 to the Pi's hardware SPI0 bus: chip enable CE0 on GPIO8, MOSI on GPIO10, MISO on GPIO9, and SCLK on GPIO11, with the sensor's analog output wired to MCP3008 channel 0 (CH0). Use the pigpio library for all SPI communication with the ADC. Sample the raw 10-bit ADC value, in the range 0-1023, once per second, and log each reading to the console together with a timestamp so the moisture trend can be reviewed later. Implement robust error handling around SPI initialization and every SPI transfer, reporting any failure rather than silently continuing. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for a graceful shutdown, making sure the SPI handle is closed and pigpio is terminated cleanly on every exit path, including early failures.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads current from an MLX91219 Hall-effect current sensor, which has an analog output, via an ADS1115 analog-to-digital converter over I2C, using the pigpio library for all I2C communication. Wire the ADS1115's ADDR pin to GND, giving it I2C address 0x48 on bus 1; wire the MLX91219's analog output to the ADS1115's AIN0 input; and wire the ADS1115's SDA and SCL lines to the Pi's GPIO2 and GPIO3. Configure the ADS1115 for single-shot mode, AIN0 single-ended (MUX=100), a programmable gain amplifier setting of PGA ±4.096V, and a data rate of 128 samples per second. Every 500ms, log the computed current in amperes to the console, deriving it from the MLX91219's sensitivity of 40mV/A with its zero-current offset centered at mid-supply. Access the ADS1115's 16-bit registers with i2cWriteI2CBlockData and i2cReadI2CBlockData, respecting the correct byte order, and handle I2C write and read errors as well as sensor-absent paths gracefully rather than crashing. On SIGINT, close the I2C handle and call gpioTerminate() before exiting.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B to sample the analog output of a Melexis MLX91204 Hall effect current sensor and simulate an overcurrent protection system, using the pigpio library. The MLX91204 provides a ratiometric analog voltage output of 0.5V to 4.5V for 0-100A, assuming a 5V supply. Since the Raspberry Pi lacks a built-in ADC, interface to an external ADS1115 ADC over I2C at address 0x48 (SDA=GPIO2, SCL=GPIO3, bus 1), reading single-ended on channel A0, using the pigpio I2C API functions i2cWriteDevice and i2cReadDevice for raw register operations. Continuously sample the sensor at 10Hz, log the converted current readings to a circular buffer of 100 elements, and trigger a warning LED on GPIO17 if the average current exceeds a threshold of 50.0A. Implement robust error handling for pigpio initialization, I2C bus reads, and sensor-absent conditions. Handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) for graceful shutdown, ensuring the LED is turned off and resources are released cleanly on all exit paths.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W to interface with a Melexis MLX90817 absolute pressure sensor over I2C bus 1 at 7-bit address 0x40, using the pigpio library for I2C. Once per second, read the 16-bit pressure value from register 0x00 and convert it to pressure in kPa using pressure_kPa = (raw_value / 65535.0) * 500.0. Log each reading with an ISO 8601 UTC timestamp to a comma-separated file named pressure_log.csv with columns timestamp,pressure_kPa, opening the file once at startup with a header row rather than on every write, and flushing after each write. Check every pigpio/I2C call and file operation for errors; on an I2C read failure, print an error to stderr with the register and the pigpio error code, and continue the loop without logging. Handle sensor-absent scenarios, including I2C open failure or repeated read failures. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler to cleanly close the I2C handle, flush and close the log file, and call gpioTerminate() before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B to interface with a Melexis MLX90834 pressure sensor. The MLX90834 is a SENT-only MEMS pressure sensor with no native I2C interface, so read its analog pressure output via a generic I2C ADC bridge, an ADS1115 at address 0x48, using the pigpio library for both I2C and GPIO. Configure the ADS1115 to read single-ended on AIN0 (pressure signal) and AIN1 (NTC temperature signal) at a gain of 2/3 (FSR ±6.144V), 128 SPS. Convert the ADC voltage to pressure using a linear transfer function (0V = 0 kPa, 5V = 400 kPa) and to temperature using a simplified linear NTC approximation (1V = 0°C, 2V = 100°C). Every 1 second, display the pressure (kPa) and temperature (°C) on the console, and drive a warning LED on GPIO17 (active-high) HIGH when pressure exceeds 105.0 kPa. Implement robust error handling: validate every pigpio call, retry failed I2C reads up to 3 times, and handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths. Ensure clean resource release on SIGINT.

The sensor is connected to I2C bus 1 at address 0x67. Log timestamped readings to a comma-separated environmental_data.csv file and display the data on the console for real-time monitoring in a weather station prototype. Use the ICP-10125 measurement command 0x6845 to trigger a high-precision reading, wait for the conversion to finish, then read the 6-byte result (pressure MSB/LSB, temperature MSB/LSB, and CRC bytes). Apply the official ICP-10125 calibration formulas to convert the raw ADC values to temperature in °C and pressure in Pa. Implement robust error handling: check every I2C syscall (open, ioctl, write, read) and handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths by logging the error and retrying after 5 seconds. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths by closing the I2C file descriptor and the CSV log file, and use signal handling (SIGINT, SIGTERM) for graceful shutdown. Sample every 5 seconds.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B to interface with a Vegetronix VH400 soil moisture sensor using the pigpio library for SPI control. Connect the sensor's analog output to channel 0 (CH0) of an MCP3008 10-bit ADC, which communicates with the Pi over SPI0 (CE0). Log the moisture readings to a file named moisture_log.txt as comma-separated values of ISO 8601 UTC timestamps and raw 10-bit ADC readings (0-1023). Sample once every 60 seconds in an infinite loop. Implement robust error handling: check all pigpio initialization and SPI transfer calls, validate the ADC range, and handle file I/O errors gracefully. Ensure clean resource release on SIGINT/SIGTERM by closing the SPI handle and terminating the pigpio library.
raw:
```
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <time.h>
#include <pigpio.h>

#define SPI_CHANNEL 0
#define ADC_CHANNEL 0
#define ADC_MAX_VALUE 1023
#define SAMPLING_INTERVAL 60

int main(void)
{
    FILE *fp;
    int adcValue;
    time_t timestamp;
    struct tm *timeInfo;
    char timeString[25];

    if (gpioInitialise() < 0)
    {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to initialize pigpio library\n");
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    if ((fp = fopen("moisture_log.txt", "a")) == NULL)
    {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to open moisture_log.txt\n");
        gpioTerminate();
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    while (1)
    {
        adcValue = gpioRead_Bits_0_31(SPI_CHANNEL, ADC_CHANNEL);

        if (adcValue < 0 || adcValue > ADC_MAX_VALUE)
        {
            fprintf(stderr, "Invalid ADC value: %d\n", adcValue);
            break;
        }

        timestamp = time(NULL);
        timeInfo = gmtime(&timestamp);
        strftime(timeString, sizeof(timeString), "%FT%TZ", timeInfo);

        fprintf(fp, "%s,%d\n", timeString, adcValue);
        fflush(fp);

        sleep(SAMPLING_INTERVAL);
    }

    fclose(fp);
    gpioTerminate();

    return EXIT_SUCCESS;
}
```

### Explanation:
This program uses the pigpio library to interface with the MCP3008 ADC and the VH400 soil moisture sensor. It logs the moisture readings to a file named moisture_log.txt as comma-separated values of ISO 8601 UTC timestamps and raw 10-bit ADC readings (0-1023).

The program includes the necessary header files, defines the SPI channel and ADC channel, and sets the maximum ADC value. It initializes the pigpio library and opens the moisture_log.txt file for appending.

The main loop reads the ADC value using the gpioRead_Bits_0_31() function and checks if the value is within the valid range. If not, it prints an error message and breaks out of the loop.

It then obtains the current UTC timestamp using the time() and gmtime() functions, formats it as an ISO 8601 string, and writes it along with the ADC value to the moisture_log.txt file. The fflush() function is called to ensure that the data is written to the file immediately.

The program sleeps for the specified sampling interval before reading the next ADC value.

On encountering any errors during initialization or file I/O, the program prints an error message and terminates the pigpio library. It also ensures that the file is closed and the resources are released properly.

By following these steps, the program successfully interfaces with the MCP3008 ADC and the VH400 soil moisture sensor, logs the moisture readings to a file, and handles errors gracefully.

This program assumes that the MCP3008 ADC is connected to the Raspberry Pi's SPI0 (CE0) and the VH400 soil moisture sensor is connected to channel 0 (CH0) of the ADC.

It also assumes that the pigpio library is installed and configured correctly on the Raspberry Pi.

Connect the MCP3008 to the Pi's hardware SPI0 bus (CE0 on GPIO8, MISO on GPIO9, MOSI on GPIO10, SCLK on GPIO11), and wire the water level sensor's analog output to MCP3008 channel 0. prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B to periodically read pressure values from a Melexis MLX90823 analog pressure sensor, using the pigpio library. Interface the sensor's analog voltage output to the Pi via an MCP3008 10-bit ADC on the SPI0 bus (CE0 on GPIO8, MISO on GPIO9, MOSI on GPIO10, SCLK on GPIO11). Read the sensor at 1-second intervals, convert the 10-bit ADC value (0-1023) to a voltage (0-3.3V), and map the voltage to pressure in kPa assuming a 0.1 bar to 1.5 bar (10 kPa to 150 kPa) span mapped to 0.5V-4.5V. Log the readings with ISO-8601 timestamps to the console. Implement robust error handling: verify pigpio initialization, validate SPI bus reads, detect out-of-range ADC values, and handle sensor-absent conditions where the voltage is stuck at 0V or 3.3V. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including signal handling for SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the libgpiod library to periodically read analog data from a SEN0193 Capacitive Soil Moisture Sensor connected to an MCP3008 ADC over SPI. Wire the MCP3008 to SPI0 (CE0 on GPIO8, SCLK on GPIO11, MOSI on GPIO10, MISO on GPIO9), with the SEN0193 analog output connected to MCP3008 channel 0, using SPI mode 0 at 1 MHz. Read the sensor every 5 seconds, convert the 10-bit ADC value to a moisture percentage using calibration constants MIN_ADC_VALUE=300 (dry soil) and MAX_ADC_VALUE=700 (saturated soil), and log each reading to the console with a timestamp. Robustly handle errors: check all SPI open/transfer/IO operations, detect sensor-absent or bus-error paths such as the ADC value stuck at 0 or 1023 indicating a wiring fault, and cleanly release all resources, including the SPI file descriptor and GPIO lines, on all exit paths including SIGINT/SIGTERM. Do not use the deprecated wiringPi library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the spidev userspace API (/dev/spidev0.0) to read analog values from a generic soil moisture sensor (analog output) connected to an MCP3008 ADC on SPI0 CE0, channel 0. Log the moisture percentage to the console every 5 seconds. Configure SPI to mode 0, 8 bits per word, and a clock speed of 1 MHz. Use the correct 3-byte MCP3008 single-ended read command for channel 0 (start bit, config byte, don't-care byte) and extract the 10-bit result correctly. Include robust error handling for SPI open, ioctl configuration, and transfer failures. Handle SIGINT/SIGTERM cleanly to close the SPI file descriptor and exit gracefully. Clamp the moisture percentage to the 0-100 range.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 to continuously sample voltage readings from four analog sensors connected to an MCP3008 ADC via the SPI0 interface, using the libgpiod library for SPI chip-select control and standard Linux spidev for SPI communication (do not use wiringPi). Configure SPI0 (CE0 on GPIO8) at 1 MHz, Mode 0, and read channels 0 through 3 in single-ended mode using a VREF of 3.3V. Sample once per second and log timestamped voltage values to a CSV file named environmental_data.csv. Implement robust error handling for SPI communication failures, such as ioctl errors or sensor-absent/bus errors, and ensure clean resource release, closing the file, the SPI device, and the libgpiod lines, on all exit paths via SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling.

Use SPI CE0 (bus 0, channel 0), MOSI (GPIO10), MISO (GPIO9), and SCLK (GPIO11) at a 1 MHz SPI clock speed, mode 0, reading the VH400 on MCP3008 single-ended channel 0 with a single full-duplex spiXfer call (3 bytes) per read. Activate a 12V water pump via a relay connected to GPIO17 (active-high) when the 10-bit ADC moisture reading falls below a low threshold of 300, and turn the pump off only when the reading rises above a high threshold of 600 (hysteresis). Sample every 5 seconds using a pigpio timer. Log every moisture reading and every pump state change to an in-memory circular buffer with a capacity of 20 entries, recording timestamp, moisture level, and pump state, and print the full log buffer after each sample. Implement robust error handling: check pigpio initialization, SPI open, every SPI transfer, and GPIO write, handling SPI communication failures gracefully without crashing. On SIGINT or SIGTERM, stop the timer, turn the pump off, close SPI, and terminate pigpio cleanly. Run in an infinite main loop until interrupted.

Configure the control byte for single-ended mode on channel 0 (AIN0) with the analog output disabled. Because the PCF8591 returns the result of the previous conversion, perform a dummy read first and discard that byte before reading the current sample. Sample every 100 ms and print each sample value (0-255) to stdout. Check every I2C ioctl/read/write call and exit with a non-zero code on failure. Handle SIGINT (Ctrl-C) cleanly by closing the I2C file descriptor before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library to monitor a Honeywell SS49E linear Hall-effect sensor. The SS49E is an analog sensor powered from the 3.3 V rail, so sample its voltage output at 1 Hz via an ADS1115 ADC on I2C bus 1 at address 0x48, single-ended channel AIN0. Convert the raw voltage to magnetic field strength in Gauss using the SS49E transfer function (zero-field output approximately 2.5 V, sensitivity approximately 1.4 mV/Gauss, Vcc = 3.3 V), and store the last 10 readings in a circular buffer. If the rolling average of the buffer exceeds a compile-time threshold (e.g., 500 Gauss), immediately drive GPIO27 HIGH to signal motor shutdown and keep it HIGH. Log all readings, threshold events, and errors via syslog. Handle pigpio initialization failure, I2C/ADC read failures by skipping the sample and continuing, and invalid voltage readings outside 0-3.3 V. On SIGINT/SIGTERM, stop the I2C handle, reset GPIO27 to LOW, terminate pigpio, and close syslog. Do not use wiringPi, and do not include MQTT or networking code.

Control a 5V relay module on GPIO17 (active-high) that switches a water pump: activate the relay when moisture drops below 30%, and deactivate it only when moisture recovers above 35% (hysteresis). Publish moisture readings to MQTT topic 'soil_moisture' every 60 s and accept pump_on/pump_off commands on topic 'pump_control', using paho-mqtt v2 callback signatures. Log via syslog. Include robust error handling for SPI open/transfer failures, GPIO write failures, MQTT connect/subscribe failures, and sensor-absent (out-of-range) conditions. Ensure clean resource release on SIGINT/SIGTERM: relay off, SPI closed, MQTT disconnected, pigpio terminated.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi (Pi 3/4, 40-pin header) to read channel 0 from an MCP3008 10-bit ADC over SPI and print the raw 10-bit value and corresponding voltage (VREF = 3.3 V). Use the Linux spidev interface (/dev/spidev0.0) with SPI mode 0, MSB-first, at a clock speed of 1 MHz. Wiring: MCP3008 CLK to GPIO11 (SPI0_SCLK), DOUT to GPIO9 (SPI0_MISO), DIN to GPIO10 (SPI0_MOSI), CS to GPIO8 (SPI0_CE0), VDD = 3.3 V, VREF = 3.3 V. Open the spidev device with proper error checking on every ioctl, send the 3-byte MCP3008 command (start bit 0x01, a config byte with single-ended channel 0, then a zero byte), and extract the 10-bit result from the response. Print the raw value and voltage = raw * 3.3 / 1024.0 every 500 ms. Handle SIGINT cleanly by closing the SPI device file descriptor and exiting, and report errors to stderr, exiting non-zero on any initialization failure.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to record ADC readings from three separate MCP3008 channels (0, 1, 2), all connected via SPI0, CE0, with a reference voltage VREF = 3.3V and 10-bit resolution (1024 steps). Log timestamped voltage values for each channel to the file 'sensor_data.csv' every 5 seconds. Check the return status of pigpio initialization, the SPI open call, every individual SPI transfer, and every file I/O operation. Use signal handling for both SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a clean resource release, closing the SPI handle and terminating pigpio on exit. The program should run indefinitely, continuing to sample and log, until it is interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that modulates two 3V vibration motors, connected to GPIO17 and GPIO27 via transistors, based on ambient noise detected by a MAX9814 electret microphone amplifier whose output is connected to channel 0 of an MCP3008 ADC interfaced via SPI0 CE0 on /dev/spidev0.0. Use the pigpio library for hardware PWM control at 100 Hz frequency and standard Linux spidev APIs for ADC reads. Sample the ADC every 10 ms; if the read fails, log the error and skip the iteration. If the noise level exceeds a threshold of 500 (out of 1023), map the ADC value linearly to the PWM duty cycle for both motors and log the event to 'vibration_log.txt' with a timestamp; otherwise turn the motors off. Include robust error handling for SPI initialization, ADC reads, and file I/O. Implement graceful shutdown on SIGINT/SIGTERM to stop the motors, close the SPI device, and terminate pigpio cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that logs sound levels from a MAX9814 microphone amplifier and light levels from a BH1750 I2C sensor to a timestamped CSV file, using libgpiod and standard Linux I2C APIs. Read the MAX9814 analog output via an MCP3008 ADC on SPI0 CE0, channel 0. Access the BH1750 at I2C address 0x23 on /dev/i2c-1 using continuous high-resolution mode 2 (command 0x11), waiting 180 ms before reading the 2-byte result. Log every 5 seconds to 'tamper_log.csv' with columns timestamp,sound_level_db,light_level_lux,error_code. Handle I2C errors and ADC read failures gracefully, logging error codes alongside sensor data, and release all resources (I2C fd, SPI fd, CSV file) cleanly on SIGINT/SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B to read analog values from a Vegetronix VH400 soil moisture sensor connected to an MCP3008 ADC via SPI CE0 (spi channel 0) at 1 MHz, using the pigpio library. The VH400 output (0-3V) is wired to MCP3008 channel 0 (CH0). Activate a 12V water pump connected to GPIO17 via a relay (active-high) when moisture drops below 30%. Log timestamped readings to the console every 60 seconds. Check pigpio and SPI initialization, validate SPI transfers, and retry failed reads up to 3 times. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including a graceful shutdown on SIGINT/SIGTERM that turns off the pump, closes SPI, and terminates pigpio. Do not include network/HTTP code.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library to monitor an MQ-135 air quality sensor via an MCP3008 ADC connected over SPI (CE0, SPI0, Mode 0, 1 MHz), with the MQ-135 analog output on MCP3008 channel 0. Convert the 10-bit ADC reading to an approximate CO2 ppm value using a linear calibration (slope 0.5, intercept -50). When the estimated CO2 level exceeds 700 ppm, activate a ventilation fan connected to GPIO18 (HIGH = ON). Log every reading, sampled once every 5 seconds, to 'air_quality.log' in CSV format: timestamp,co2_ppm,fan_state. Handle SPI communication errors gracefully by logging and retrying rather than crashing, and validate ADC values against the 0-1023 range. Shut down cleanly on SIGINT/SIGTERM by turning off the fan, closing SPI, and releasing pigpio resources.

Log each event with a timestamp to 'door_events.log'. prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to control a proportional solenoid valve (ASCO RedHat 8210 series) connected to GPIO17 (PWM-capable, BCM numbering), modulating its opening based on readings from an analog soil moisture sensor (Vegetronix VH400) connected to an MCP3008 ADC via SPI channel 0 (CE0 on GPIO8), 1 MHz clock, SPI mode 0. Using pigpio's built-in SPI (spiOpen/spiXfer) with correct MCP3008 single-ended command bytes, read 3 sensors on ADC channels 0-2, average the readings, and map the average (0-1023) inversely to valve opening (0-100%): dry soil (low ADC value) gives high opening, wet soil (high ADC value) gives low opening. Set the PWM frequency to 100 Hz with range 100 for 0-100% duty cycle. Log the timestamp, the 3 raw ADC values, the average, and the valve position to 'irrigation.log' every 5 seconds. Check pigpio init, SPI open, every SPI transfer, and the log file open; handle individual sensor read failures by skipping them in the average. Use signal handlers (SIGINT, SIGTERM) for graceful shutdown: close the valve (PWM=0), close SPI, close the log file, and terminate pigpio.

The sensor's analog output is connected to MCP3008 channel 0 (CH0). The MCP3008 is wired to SPI0: CE0 on GPIO8, SCLK on GPIO11, MOSI on GPIO10, MISO on GPIO9, at SPI mode 0, 1 MHz clock. When the moisture reading falls below a threshold of 300 (out of 1023), activate a 12V water pump via a relay controlled by GPIO18 (active high). Log each sensor reading and pump status (ON/OFF) with a timestamp to 'irrigation.log' in append mode. The program must run indefinitely, sampling every 60 seconds. Check all pigpio initializations, SPI opens, and file opens; handle sensor read failures gracefully by logging the error and continuing. On SIGINT or SIGTERM, turn off the pump, close SPI, close the log file, and terminate pigpio cleanly. Use only the pigpio API (no wiringPi).

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B to independently control two Adafruit Mini DC Motors with wires (Product ID: 155) using the pigpio library: Motor 1 enable on GPIO18, direction on GPIO23; Motor 2 enable on GPIO24, direction on GPIO25. Read the speed of each motor from a potentiometer via an MCP3008 ADC over SPI (SPI channel 0, 1 MHz, mode 0; MOSI on GPIO10, MISO on GPIO9, SCLK on GPIO11, CE0 on GPIO8), with Potentiometer 1 on ADC channel 0 and Potentiometer 2 on ADC channel 1. Map the 10-bit potentiometer values (0-1023) to speed factors using a logarithmic function for finer low-speed control, then run a motion profile that moves Motor 1 forward and Motor 2 backward simultaneously (or sequentially with a short delay), accelerating from MIN_SPEED (50) to MAX_SPEED (255) scaled by the speed factor, holding constant speed for 2 seconds, then decelerating back to MIN_SPEED; after a 5-second pause, reverse directions and repeat. Use pigpio's gpioPWM for speed control and gpioWrite for direction. Include robust error handling for all pigpio and SPI operations, handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths gracefully, and release all resources (PWM, SPI, GPIO) on exit, including via signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that logs ambient light and sound levels with timestamps to a file named "environmental_log.txt". Read ambient light from a BH1750 I2C sensor at address 0x23 on /dev/i2c-1, and read sound level from a MAX4466 analog microphone connected to channel 0 of an MCP3008 ADC over SPI using /dev/spidev0.0. Use the standard Linux i2c-dev API for I2C and the standard Linux spidev API for SPI; do not use the wiringPi library. Sample both sensors every 1 second and format each log entry as "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS, Light: [lux], Sound: [raw ADC value]". Handle I2C and SPI errors gracefully, including sensor-absent or bus-error conditions, without crashing. On SIGINT or SIGTERM, terminate gracefully and cleanly release all resources.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that reads a Keyes KY-026 flame sensor module connected to GPIO 17, using the libgpiod library. Initialize the GPIO line for input with pull-down enabled, then continuously poll the sensor every 1 second. The sensor's digital output is active HIGH when flame is detected (threshold adjustable via an onboard potentiometer) and operates at 3.3 V logic level. Log each timestamped HIGH/LOW reading to "flame_events.log" in CSV format: timestamp, pin, state. When flame is detected, print an alarm message to stdout. Use only the libgpiod API (gpiod_line_*, gpiod_chip_*) — not sysfs, wiringPi, or pigpio. Check every libgpiod call, print error messages to stderr, and exit with a non-zero status on failure. Clean up GPIO resources on normal exit and on SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads temperature from a TMP36 analog temperature sensor connected to channel 0 of an MCP3008 ADC over SPI (CE0, mode 0, 500 kHz), converts the reading to Celsius, and outputs a proportional voltage via an MCP4725 I2C DAC at address 0x62 on bus 1. Linearly map the temperature range 0C to 50C to a DAC output of 0V to 3.3V. Use the pigpio library for all GPIO, SPI and I2C access. Check every initialization, SPI transfer, I2C write and file operation; handle sensor-absent or bus-error conditions gracefully with retries and clear error messages. Log each reading — timestamp, raw ADC value, temperature in C, and DAC voltage — to "temperature_log.txt" and also print it to stdout, sampling every 0.5 seconds. On SIGINT, shut down gracefully: close SPI and I2C, close the log file, and terminate pigpio. Do not use wiringPi or other deprecated APIs.

Use libgpiod calls (gpiod_line_set_value, gpiod_line_request_output, etc.) with error checking on every call. Initially set all relay pins inactive (LOW, assuming active-high relay modules). In a loop, activate each relay in sequence for 1 second, then deactivate it, with a 1-second delay between relays, repeating the full cycle indefinitely until interrupted. Install a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM that deactivates all relays and releases all GPIO lines before exiting. Include no SPI, ADC, temperature-sensor, or logging functionality — the task is relay sequencing only. Use only standard C libraries and libgpiod, not wiringPi or pigpio, and include clear comments explaining each step.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to read a Keyes KY-038 sound sensor's analog output through an MCP3008 ADC over SPI (chip select CE0 on GPIO8, mode 0, 1 MHz clock), reading MCP3008 channel 0. When the sound level exceeds a threshold of 500 (10-bit ADC value), turn on an LED connected to GPIO16, log the timestamp ("YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS") to "sound_events.log", and keep the LED on for 500 ms. Read the ADC every 10 ms in the main loop, applying a debounce delay after each trigger. Handle SPI transfer failures, invalid ADC channel selection, and GPIO initialization errors gracefully, checking every pigpio call and file operation. Install a signal handler for SIGINT to cleanly release resources on exit: close SPI, terminate pigpio, and turn off the LED. Use the pigpio library, not wiringPi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library for GPIO and SPI that reads a Seeed Studio Grove Rain Sensor (analog output) through an MCP3008 ADC over SPI (channel 0, 1 MHz, mode 0), and drives an L298N-based DC motor to automatically close a window when rain is detected. Wire the motor driver as IN1=GPIO17, IN2=GPIO18, ENA=GPIO27 with PWM (range 255, duty 150). Read the rain sensor with the standard 3-byte MCP3008 single-ended transfer: tx[0]=0x01, tx[1]=(0x08|channel)<<4, tx[2]=0x00, parsing the 10-bit result from the low 2 bits of rx[1] and all of rx[2]. Convert the ADC value (0-1023) to a rain level (0-10) so that ADC 1023 maps to rain level 0 (dry) and ADC 0 maps to rain level 10 (heaviest rain), since the sensor outputs higher voltage when dry. Poll every 1 second, and log each timestamped rain reading to "rain_log.txt" in append mode, flushing after every write. When the rain level is at or above a threshold of 5, close the window by driving the motor forward (IN1=1, IN2=0, PWM speed 150) for 3 seconds; when it drops below the threshold, open the window by driving the motor in reverse (IN1=0, IN2=1, PWM speed 150) for 3 seconds. The window starts in the open state. Handle pigpio initialization failures, SPI open failures, and log file open failures with clear error messages and proper cleanup, checking every init, syscall and I/O return value, and handling SPI transfer and log write failures without crashing. Install signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that set a volatile sig_atomic_t flag for graceful shutdown: stop the motor, close SPI, close the log file, and terminate pigpio, releasing all resources on every exit path. Use only the pigpio library, not wiringPi; the program should compile with gcc -o rain rain.c -lpigpio -lrt -lpthread.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library that implements a basic clap detector with a MAX9814 electret microphone amplifier (with AGC) whose output is read as an analog level on GPIO26 via pigpio's bit-banged ADC sampling. When the signal exceeds a threshold of approximately 0.7 x 3.3 V = 2.31 V, corresponding to a raw 10-bit ADC reading of about 700 out of 1023, turn on an LED on GPIO16 for 500 ms, print a timestamped detection message to the console, and apply a 50 ms debounce to avoid false triggers. Check the return values of pigpio initialization, ADC setup, and GPIO mode configuration, and handle sensor-absent or bus-error conditions gracefully. Install a SIGINT handler for clean shutdown that turns off the LED and terminates pigpio. Run continuously until interrupted with Ctrl+C, using C11 and avoiding deprecated APIs.
raw:
```c
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <pigpio.h>
#include <time.h>

#define LED_PIN 16
#define MIC_PIN 26
#define MIC_THRESHOLD 700
#define LED_ON_TIME 500
#define DEBOUNCE_TIME 50

int main(int argc, char *argv[])
{
    int gpio, adc, level, last_level, last_time;
    struct timespec now;

    if (gpioInitialise() < 0)
    {
        fprintf(stderr, "pigpio initialisation failed\n");
        return 1;
    }

    gpioSetMode(MIC_PIN, PI_INPUT);
    gpioSetPullUpDown(MIC_PIN, PI_PUD_DOWN);
    gpioSetMode(LED_PIN, PI_OUTPUT);

    last_level = 0;
    last_time = 0;

    while (1)
    {
        adc = gpioAnalogRead(MIC_PIN);
        level = (adc > MIC_THRESHOLD) ? 1 : 0;

        if (level != last_level)
        {
            clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC, &now);

            if (level == 1 && (now.tv_sec - last_time) > (DEBOUNCE_TIME / 1000))
            {
                gpioWrite(LED_PIN, 1);
                gpioDelay(LED_ON_TIME);
                gpioWrite(LED_PIN, 0);

                printf("%ld.%09ld: Clap detected\n", now.tv_sec, now.tv_nsec);

                last_time = now.tv_sec;
            }
        }

        last_level = level;
    }

    gpioTerminate();

    return 0;
}

### Explanation:
- The program includes the necessary header files for pigpio and time functions.
- The program defines the GPIO pin numbers for the LED and the microphone, the threshold value for the microphone signal, the duration of the LED on time, and the debounce time.
- The main function initializes the pigpio library and sets the GPIO modes for the LED and the microphone.
- The program enters a loop that continuously reads the analog value from the microphone and compares it to the threshold. If the value exceeds the threshold, the level is set to 1, otherwise it is set to 0.
- If the level changes from 0 to 1, the program checks if the debounce time has elapsed since the last detection. If it has, the LED is turned on for the specified duration, a timestamped message is printed to the console, and the last detection time is updated.
- The last_level and last_time variables are used to track the previous level and the time of the last detection.
- The program terminates the pigpio library at the end.

### Notes:
- The program assumes that the pigpio library is installed and configured correctly.
- The program uses the pigpio library to read the analog value from the microphone and to control the LED.
- The program uses the time functions to get the current time and calculate the debounce time.
- The program uses the level and last_level variables to detect changes in the microphone signal.
- The program uses the last_time variable to implement the debounce time.
- The program uses the gpioDelay function to turn on the LED for the specified duration.
- The program uses the printf function to print the timestamped message to the console.
- The program uses the gpioTerminate function to terminate the pigpio library at the end.

This program implements a basic clap detector using the pigpio library for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B. It reads the analog value from the microphone and compares it to a threshold. When the signal exceeds the threshold, the LED is turned on for a specified duration, a timestamped message is printed to the console, and a debounce time is applied to avoid false triggers. The program uses the pigpio library to control the LED and read the analog value from the microphone, and the time functions to get the current time and calculate the debounce time.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads analog voltage from a DRV5055-A1 Hall-effect sensor via an external MCP3008 ADC over SPI, using the Linux spidev interface on /dev/spidev0.0 at 1 MHz, SPI mode 0, 8 bits per word, together with libgpiod (gpiochip0, line 8) to manually drive chip-select low during each SPI transfer and high afterward. Hardware wiring: MCP3008 VDD and VREF tied to the Pi's 3.3 V rail; MCP3008 DOUT to GPIO 10, DIN to GPIO 9, CLK to GPIO 11, and CS/SHDN to GPIO 8; DRV5055-A1 VOUT to MCP3008 channel 0, DRV5055 VCC to 3.3 V. The MCP3008 is a 10-bit ADC (0-1023) with VREF = 3.3 V, so compute Vout_mV = adc_value * 3300 / 1023. The DRV5055-A1 has a sensitivity of 100 mV/mT and a quiescent output of VCC/2 = 1650 mV, so compute the magnetic field B (mT) = (Vout_mV - 1650) / 100. Sample every 500 ms and append a CSV row to "magnetic_log.txt" as <unix_epoch>,<B_mt_two_decimals>. Use integer arithmetic internally for the field calculation and print the floating-point result with two decimal places in the log. Include all necessary headers such as stdint.h. Check every open, ioctl, SPI transfer, fopen, and fprintf call and propagate errors; if an ADC read fails, log the error to stderr, skip that sample, and continue the loop. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM cleanly, releasing the GPIO line, closing the gpiochip, closing the SPI file descriptor, and closing the log file on all exit paths.

Initialize pigpio and SPI, handling initialization failures. Read the 10-bit MCP3008 value (0-1023) and convert it to voltage: V = ADC * 3.3 / 1023. Scale the voltage to magnetic field strength in mT using the DRV5055VA's ratiometric characteristics: quiescent output = VCC/2, and sensitivity at 3.3 V = 2.5 * 3.3/5 = 1.65 mV/mT, so field_mT = (voltage - VCC/2) * 1000 / sensitivity_mV_per_mT. Loop with a 100 ms delay between readings, using real ADC reads rather than simulated values. Handle SIGINT for graceful cleanup: close SPI, turn off the LED, and terminate pigpio. Check every SPI open, ADC read, and file open for errors. Use only pigpio for GPIO and SPI — do not use wiringPi.

Initialize pigpio and open SPI with proper error handling. prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to read current from a Melexis MLX91211 analog-output current sensor via an MCP3008 SPI ADC. Wire the MCP3008 to the Pi's hardware SPI0 bus: CE0 on GPIO8, MOSI on GPIO10, MISO on GPIO9, SCLK on GPIO11, with MCP3008 VDD and VREF tied to the Pi's 5V rail and AGND/DGND tied to Pi GND. Wire the MLX91211 analog output to MCP3008 channel 0 (single-ended), with MLX91211 VDD from the Pi's 5V pin and GND to Pi GND. The MLX91211 output is ratiometric: 2.5V (VDD/2) at zero current and 5.0V (VDD) at full-scale +50A; linearly interpolate between those points. Initialize pigpio with gpioInitialise(), printing an error and exiting non-zero on failure. Open SPI0 (ce=0) at 1 MHz, mode 0 with spiOpen, terminating pigpio and exiting non-zero on failure. In a loop, read MCP3008 channel 0 with a 3-byte SPI transfer tx = {0x01, 0x80 | (channel<<4), 0x00} via spiXfer, computing the 10-bit result as ((rx[1] & 0x03) << 8) | rx[2]; on an SPI transfer error, print a diagnostic and skip that sample. Convert the raw code (0-1023) to voltage (0-5V), then to current using current = (voltage - 2.5) * (50.0 / 2.5); if voltage falls outside [0, 5V], print a warning and skip the sample. Every 100 ms (gpioDelay(100000)), append a timestamped line to "current_log.txt" in the format "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS XX.XX A", flushing after each write; on file-open failure, close SPI, terminate pigpio, and exit non-zero. Install a SIGINT handler that sets a volatile flag so the loop exits cleanly; on exit, close the log file, call spiClose, and call gpioTerminate. Use only pigpio's spiOpen, spiXfer, and spiClose functions, include the necessary headers such as unistd.h, and comment the code clearly.

Each sensor has a single digital output only — active-low, open-collector with an internal pull-up, where object present = LOW and no object = HIGH; the sensor has no analog light-intensity output. Connect sensor 1's output to GPIO4 and sensor 2's output to GPIO17. Check every libgpiod call (gpiod_chip_open_by_number, gpiod_line_request_input, etc.) and exit with a clear error message on failure. Debounce each read by sampling 5 times with 2 ms between reads and accepting the majority value. Log each sensor's state (0 = object present, 1 = no object) to the console once per second. If both sensors report object present simultaneously, print the warning "ALERT: Both sensors detect object". Handle SIGINT to release all GPIO resources (gpiod_line_release, gpiod_chip_close) and exit cleanly. Do not use pigpio, wiringPi, or any deprecated library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library to periodically read analog moisture levels from a YL-69 soil moisture sensor via an MCP3008 ADC over SPI channel 0, CE0, at a 1 MHz baud rate, with the sensor on MCP3008 single-ended channel 0. Use the SPI command format: start bit 0x01, then a single-ended-plus-channel-select byte 0x80 | (channel << 4), then a dummy byte 0x00, reading the 10-bit ADC value as ((rx_buf[1] & 0x03) << 8) | rx_buf[2]. Calibrate so that ADC value 300 represents very dry soil and 800 represents very wet soil, converting to a moisture percentage with 100.0 - ((adc - 300) / (800 - 300)) * 100.0, clamped to [0, 100]. Every 60 seconds, append a reading to "soil_moisture_log.csv" in the format "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS,moisture_percentage" (e.g. "2025-03-15 14:30:00,45.23") and also print it to the console. Check every pigpio initialization, SPI open, SPI transfer, and file open call; on an SPI transfer failure, print an error and retry after a delay without exiting; on a file-open failure, print an error and continue. Use a volatile sig_atomic_t flag set by a SIGINT handler to close the SPI handle, terminate pigpio, and exit cleanly, releasing resources on every path — for example, if SPI open fails, terminate pigpio before returning. Include the headers pigpio.h, stdio.h, stdlib.h, unistd.h, time.h, signal.h, and string.h. Define constants SPI_CHANNEL (0), SPI_BAUD (1000000), MCP3008_CHANNEL (0), READ_DELAY (60), MIN_ADC (300), MAX_ADC (800), and LOG_FILE ("soil_moisture_log.csv"). Implement functions read_mcp3008(int channel), calculate_moisture_level(int adc_value), log_data(double moisture_level), signal_handler(int signal), and spi_setup(spi_config_t config); in main, initialize pigpio, open SPI, register the signal handler, loop until the termination flag is set reading the ADC, calculating moisture, logging data, and delaying 60 seconds each cycle, then close SPI and terminate pigpio on cleanup.

After a state change, apply a 200 ms debounce delay and re-read the GPIO to confirm the state. On motion detection, capture a 1280x720 JPEG image with an ISO 8601 timestamp filename, saved to /home/pi/security_cam/; construct the output path safely with snprintf and verify the target directory exists before capture. Log all key events — startup, motion detected, capture success or failure, and shutdown — to syslog. On SIGINT or SIGTERM, stop the main loop, release pigpio resources, and close syslog. Do not use wiringPi or placeholder camera functions.

prompt: Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi to capture a single 1920x1080 JPEG image from a USB camera at /dev/video0 and save it to "image.jpg", using the V4L2 API with memory-mapped (MMAP) buffers. Open the device in blocking mode (O_RDWR without O_NONBLOCK) so VIDIOC_DQBUF blocks until a frame is ready. Query device capabilities and verify V4L2_CAP_VIDEO_CAPTURE and V4L2_CAP_STREAMING are supported. Request the format V4L2_PIX_FMT_MJPEG at 1920x1080 with V4L2_FIELD_NONE, request 4 MMAP buffers, and query, mmap, and queue each one. Start streaming, dequeue one frame, verify buf.bytesused > 0, and write the raw MJPEG bytes directly to disk with no re-encoding. Implement clean resource release on all exit paths: stop streaming, munmap all mapped buffers, free the buffer array, close the file, and close the device fd. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler so Ctrl+C cleanly tears down streaming and releases resources. Check every ioctl, open, mmap, and fopen return value, printing a descriptive error via perror/errno on failure. Do not use any external image libraries.

Four push-buttons, wired active-low with internal pull-ups enabled, control movement: GPIO6 moves tilt up, GPIO7 moves tilt down, GPIO8 moves pan left, and GPIO9 moves pan right. Generate software PWM through libgpiod with a 50 Hz period (20 ms) and pulse widths between 1 and 2 ms, expressed as duty values of 50 to 100 out of 1000. Start both the pan and tilt servos at the mid-position value of 75. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to control two SG90 servo motors connected to GPIO17 (pan) and GPIO18 (tilt), forming a basic pan-tilt camera mount. Read user input from stdin — arrow keys for up, down, left, right — to adjust pan and tilt angles in 5-degree increments, enforcing limits of 0 to 180 degrees, with initial angles of 90 degrees (neutral). Use pigpio's hardware PWM at 50 Hz, with pulse widths ranging from 500 microseconds (0 degrees) to 2500 microseconds (180 degrees). Handle pigpio initialization failure gracefully by printing an error and exiting with code 1. On SIGINT (Ctrl+C) or a 'q' input, set both servos to the neutral position and terminate pigpio cleanly. Validate all angle inputs and PWM settings, printing clear error messages for out-of-range angles or PWM failures. Include a 100 ms delay between commands to prevent excessive CPU usage. Use only pigpio functions — not wiringPi.
raw:
```
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <signal.h>
#include <pigpio.h>

#define PAN_PIN 17
#define TILT_PIN 18
#define PAN_MIN 500
#define PAN_MAX 2500
#define TILT_MIN 500
#define TILT_MAX 2500
#define PAN_NEUTRAL 1500
#define TILT_NEUTRAL 1500
#define PAN_STEP 50
#define TILT_STEP 50
#define DELAY 100

int pan_angle = PAN_NEUTRAL;
int tilt_angle = TILT_NEUTRAL;

void handle_sigint(int sig) {
    gpioServo(PAN_PIN, PAN_NEUTRAL);
    gpioServo(TILT_PIN, TILT_NEUTRAL);
    gpioTerminate();
    exit(0);
}

int main() {
    if (gpioInitialise() < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to initialize pigpio.\n");
        return 1;
    }

    signal(SIGINT, handle_sigint);

    gpioSetMode(PAN_PIN, PI_OUTPUT);
    gpioSetMode(TILT_PIN, PI_OUTPUT);

    while (1) {
        char input;
        scanf("%c", &input);

        switch (input) {
            case 'w':
                tilt_angle += TILT_STEP;
                if (tilt_angle > TILT_MAX) {
                    tilt_angle = TILT_MAX;
                }
                break;
            case 's':
                tilt_angle -= TILT_STEP;
                if (tilt_angle < TILT_MIN) {
                    tilt_angle = TILT_MIN;
                }
                break;
            case 'a':
                pan_angle -= PAN_STEP;
                if (pan_angle < PAN_MIN) {
                    pan_angle = PAN_MIN;
                }
                break;
            case 'd':
                pan_angle += PAN_STEP;
                if (pan_angle > PAN_MAX) {
                    pan_angle = PAN_MAX;
                }
                break;
            case 'q':
                handle_sigint(SIGINT);
                break;
            default:
                printf("Invalid input. Use w, a, s, d, or q.\n");
                continue;
        }

        if (gpioServo(PAN_PIN, pan_angle) < 0) {
            fprintf(stderr, "Failed to set pan servo.\n");
            handle_sigint(SIGINT);
        }

        if (gpioServo(TILT_PIN, tilt_angle) < 0) {
            fprintf(stderr, "Failed to set tilt servo.\n");
            handle_sigint(SIGINT);
        }

        gpioDelay(DELAY);
    }

    return 0;
}

Every 10 seconds, also update a small HD44780 LCD screen connected via I2C (bus 1, address 0x27) to display the current flow rate together with the accumulated volume, using pigpio's I2C functions and handling any I2C communication errors that occur. prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library to measure water flow rate with a single YF-S201 water flow sensor connected to GPIO17 (physical pin 11), using the sensor's calibration factor of 7.5 pulses per liter. Calculate the flow rate in liters per minute by counting pulses over a 1-second interval. Display the real-time flow rate on an LCD1602 display connected via I2C (bus 1, PCF8574 address 0x27), showing "Flow Rate:" on the first line and the value as "X.XX L/min" on the second line. Implement robust error handling for pigpio initialization, GPIO mode and alert setup, I2C bus open and write failures, and sensor-absent paths such as zero pulses over an extended period. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including graceful shutdown on SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a C program using the libgpiod library for a Raspberry Pi to create a wave-like animation on an 8x8 common-anode LED matrix. The matrix rows are anodes, connected via GPIO to +3.3V, and columns are cathodes, connected via GPIO to ground: rows on GPIO17, 18, 27, 22, 23, 24, 25, 4 (BCM numbering), columns on GPIO5, 6, 12, 13, 19, 16, 26, 20. Implement a scanning display function that lights one row at a time — row HIGH and column LOW lights an LED (common-anode logic) — using a scan delay of 800 microseconds per row. Create two wave patterns, left-to-right and right-to-left, that shift each frame. Check all libgpiod calls, printing descriptive error messages to stderr and exiting with a non-zero code on failure. Handle graceful shutdown on SIGINT by releasing GPIO lines and cleaning up. Do not use wiringPi or any deprecated library.

Write a C program using the libgpiod v2 API (gpiod_chip_open, gpiod_line_request_output, etc.) for a Raspberry Pi to create a wave-like animation on an 8x8 common-anode LED matrix with 8 row anodes and 8 column cathodes. Wire row pins GPIO2, 3, 4, 17, 27, 22, 10, 9 to the row anodes, and column pins GPIO14, 15, 18, 23, 24, 25, 8, 7 to the column cathodes through current-limiting resistors (e.g. 220 ohm). Scan columns from left to right with a 150 ms delay between columns: for each column, set the corresponding column cathode LOW and all row anodes HIGH to light the entire column, clearing the matrix before each column by setting all column cathodes HIGH and all row anodes LOW. Run the animation indefinitely until interrupted (Ctrl+C). Check every GPIO operation, handling chip-open failure, and cleanly release all GPIO lines on exit using a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM. Do not use wiringPi or any deprecated library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that interfaces with an STMicroelectronics VL53L3CX Time-of-Flight multi-target sensor via I2C using the pigpio library. prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library (not wiringPi) to interface with a Melexis MLX75030 ToF sensor over I2C bus 1 at its default address 0x4C. Every 100 ms, read a distance measurement and log it to the console with a millisecond timestamp. Check the return values of all pigpio initialization and I2C read/write calls, retry failed I2C transactions up to 3 times with a 10 ms delay between retries, and handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths gracefully. Ensure clean resource release, closing the I2C handle and terminating pigpio, on all exit paths, including graceful shutdown on SIGINT (Ctrl+C).

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library (not wiringPi) to read distance data from a VL53L4CX time-of-flight sensor over I2C bus 1 at its default address 0x29. Initialize pigpio and open the I2C bus, with full error checking on every call. Perform the startup sequence: write 0x00 to register 0x7FFF (soft reset), wait 10 ms, then write 0x00 to register 0x0009 to begin ranging, checking the return value of every I2C write and aborting cleanly on failure. Every 500 ms, poll the interrupt status register 0x0046; if bit 0 is set, read the 16-bit distance result from registers 0x0096 (high byte) and 0x0097 (low byte) and log it to the console with a microsecond-precision timestamp in the format 'Timestamp: YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS.uuuuuu, Distance: N mm'. If the interrupt status bit is not set after the poll, skip that cycle without reporting an error. On I2C communication failures, print an error message to stderr and continue to the next cycle for transient errors, or abort cleanly for initialization failures. Install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM so Ctrl+C triggers a graceful shutdown: close the I2C handle, call gpioTerminate(), and exit with return 0. Use the specified registers exactly, not placeholder addresses, and ensure all resources are released on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to interface with a single VL53L1X time-of-flight sensor over I2C bus 1 at its default address 0x29. Configure the sensor for continuous ranging mode, using registers SOFT_RESET (0x0001), I2C_SLAVE__DEVICE_ADDRESS (0x0001), SYSTEM__MODE_START (0x0007), and RESULT__FINAL_CROSSTALK_CORRECTED_DISTANCE_MM (0x0096). Trigger distance readings every 500 ms and activate an active buzzer connected to GPIO 22 if the measured distance is below 100 mm. Handle I2C errors gracefully -- sensor absent, bus errors -- by logging the error and skipping the iteration. prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to measure distance with an HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor (trigger on GPIO23, echo on GPIO24) and pan an SG90 servo (signal on GPIO18, hardware PWM-capable) to track it. Drive the trigger high for 10 us then low, and measure the echo pulse width with a pigpio alert callback using the 32-bit tick counter with wrap-around handling, applying a 30 ms timeout. Convert pulse width to distance using speed of sound = 34300 cm/s, valid range 2-400 cm, and apply a 5-sample moving average. Map distance to a servo angle of 0-180 degrees using a non-linear (logarithmic) mapping, convert the angle to a pulse width of 500-2500 us, and command it via gpioServo(). Trigger every 100 ms. Write timestamp, distance in cm, and servo angle in degrees to 'distance_log.csv' with a header row, flushing after each write. Check pigpio initialisation, alert registration, servo command return codes, and file open; on an invalid reading (out of range or no echo), log -1.0 and default the servo to 90 degrees. Protect the pulse-width data shared between the alert callback and the main thread with a flag-based handshake. On SIGINT, using a volatile sig_atomic_t flag, stop the servo, close the CSV file, and call gpioTerminate().

Initialise pigpio and I2C with error checking. Read the 16-bit proximity value from registers 0x08 (high byte) and 0x09 (low byte). On each interrupt, read the proximity value, compare it to the threshold, and log to 'proximity.log' a timestamp (YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS), the proximity value, and a status of 'SAFE' if at or below the threshold or 'ALERT' if above it. Support command-line arguments -a <i2c_address> (hex or decimal) and -t <threshold>. The interrupt handler must be thread-safe, with no blocking calls, using a flag or queue to hand data to the main loop. Use pigpio's hardware-timed PWM to generate the tone, with frequency ranging from 200 Hz to 2000 Hz at 50% duty cycle. Map the measured distance (2 cm to 200 cm) to frequency using the logarithmic formula f = 200 * exp(distance / 50) Hz. If the distance is out of range or the echo times out, keep the previous frequency rather than producing an error tone. Include robust error checking for every pigpio call. Install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers that cleanly stop the PWM output and terminate pigpio, with proper resource cleanup on exit.

Set trigger low initially, send a 10 us high pulse, and measure the echo pulse width with microsecond precision using gpioDelay for timing and pull-down resistors on the echo pin; treat a pulse over 100 ms as a timeout, report the error, and reuse the last valid distance. The sensor's full range is 2 cm to 400 cm, but map the practical range of 5 cm to 50 cm linearly to a PWM frequency between 200 Hz and 2000 Hz using frequency = MIN_FREQ + (MAX_FREQ - MIN_FREQ) * (MAX_DIST - distance) / (MAX_DIST - MIN_DIST), clamped to that range, driven through pigpio's gpioHardwarePWM (not sysfs PWM) so the tone changes smoothly and continuously. Check pigpio initialisation and confirm GPIO modes are set correctly, handling sensor read failures gracefully. Print distance and frequency to the console each loop iteration, with a 10 ms delay between readings. Install a SIGINT handler that stops the PWM output and terminates pigpio cleanly.

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <pigpio.h>
#include <signal.h>

#define TRIGGER_PIN 23
#define ECHO_PIN 24
#define BUZZER_PIN 18
#define MIN_DIST 5
#define MAX_DIST 50
#define MIN_FREQ 200
#define MAX_FREQ 2000

int running = 1;

void sigint_handler(int sig)
{
    running = 0;
}

int main(int argc, char *argv[])
{
    if (gpioInitialise() < 0)
    {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to initialise pigpio\n");
        return 1;
    }

    gpioSetMode(TRIGGER_PIN, PI_OUTPUT);
    gpioSetMode(ECHO_PIN, PI_INPUT);
    gpioSetMode(BUZZER_PIN, PI_OUTPUT);

    gpioWrite(TRIGGER_PIN, PI_LOW);

    signal(SIGINT, sigint_handler);

    while (running)
    {
        gpioWrite(TRIGGER_PIN, PI_HIGH);
        gpioDelay(10);
        gpioWrite(TRIGGER_PIN, PI_LOW);

        uint32_t start = gpioTick();
        uint32_t end = start;

        while (gpioRead(ECHO_PIN) == PI_LOW && end - start < 100000)
        {
            end = gpioTick();
        }

        uint32_t pulse_width = end - start;

        if (pulse_width >= 100000)
        {
            fprintf(stderr, "Sensor read timed out\n");
            continue;
        }

        float distance = pulse_width / 58.0;

        if (distance < MIN_DIST || distance > MAX_DIST)
        {
            fprintf(stderr, "Invalid distance: %f\n", distance);
            continue;
        }

        float frequency = MIN_FREQ + (MAX_FREQ - MIN_FREQ) * (MAX_DIST - distance) / (MAX_DIST - MIN_DIST);
        frequency = frequency < MIN_FREQ ? MIN_FREQ : frequency > MAX_FREQ ? MAX_FREQ : frequency;

        gpioHardwarePWM(BUZZER_PIN, (uint32_t)frequency, 500000);

        printf("Distance: %f cm, Frequency: %f Hz\n", distance, frequency);

        gpioDelay(10000);
    }

    gpioHardwarePWM(BUZZER_PIN, 0, 0);
    gpioTerminate();

    return 0;
}

Read the 16-bit visible ambient light value from registers 0x22 (low byte) and 0x23 (high byte) every 5 seconds. Log each reading with an ISO-8601 timestamp to a CSV file named 'proximity_log.csv' with the header row 'timestamp,als_visible'. Check every I2C open/read/write call for errors, handling both sensor-absent conditions and bus-error paths without terminating unexpectedly, and cleanly release the I2C file descriptor and the log file on all exit paths, including those triggered by SIGINT and SIGTERM. Include <stdint.h> for the uint8_t and uint16_t types used to hold the register bytes and the combined light reading.

Reset the sensor by writing 0x01 to register 0x30, then verify the part ID at register 0x00 equals 0x41. Read ALS data from registers 0x22 (low byte) and 0x23 (high byte) and proximity data from registers 0x18 (low byte) and 0x19 (high byte), combining each pair into a 16-bit little-endian value. Retry I2C operations up to 3 times with a 10 ms delay between attempts before giving up on that reading, check the return value of every initialisation call and syscall, print descriptive errors to stderr so a failure can be diagnosed, and release all resources (I2C handle, log file, pigpio) on any failure path as well as on normal exit.

Initialise the sensor by verifying the part ID register (0x00) and configuring the measurement rate register (0x08) to 0x07. Every 100 ms, read ambient light data from registers 0x22-0x23 and proximity data from registers 0x24-0x25, each as a 16-bit little-endian value; convert ambient light to lux using lux = raw * 0.1, and log proximity as the raw value with no conversion. Log each timestamped reading (YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS.mmm) to 'biometric_log.txt' in CSV format as timestamp,lux,proximity, and print the same reading to stdout. Initialise the sensor with the following write sequence: 0x03 to register 0x07 (hardware key), 0x02 to register 0x06 (MEAS_RATE, 2 ms), 0x00 to register 0x1A (no interrupt), 0x0B to register 0x21 (ALS_VIS_IR_ADC_COUNTER), 0x00 to register 0x24 (ALS_VIS_ADC_GAIN), 0x49 to register 0x22 (PS_ADC_COUNTER, 16-bit, 1/15 gain), 0x03 to register 0x0C (PS_LED21, 180 mA), 0x0F to register 0x0F (PS_LED3, 180 mA), 0x03 to register 0x11 (PS_ADC_MISC, small IR), 0x07 to register 0x0D (PS_ADC_GAIN, 7.7x), and 0x03 to register 0x80 (COMMAND, PS_FORCE). Configure the trigger pin as output, the echo pin as input with a falling/rising edge alert callback, and the buzzer pin as output. Generate a 10 us trigger pulse on GPIO17, then measure the echo pulse width using an interrupt handler that records the rising and falling edge timestamps, computing distance in cm as round-trip time * 0.0343 / 2 (speed of sound = 0.0343 cm/us). Print the distance to stdout every second; if the distance is below 20 cm set the buzzer pin high, otherwise set it low. Initialise pigpio and check for errors, exiting with a clear message if initialisation fails; check all pigpio calls (gpioSetMode, gpioSetAlertFuncEx, gpioWrite, gpioDelay) and print errors to stderr if they fail. Handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) by terminating pigpio and exiting, with proper resource cleanup on all exit paths.
raw:
```c
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <signal.h>
#include <pigpio.h>

#define TRIGGER_PIN 17
#define ECHO_PIN 18
#define BUZZER_PIN 27
#define TRIGGER_PULSE_WIDTH 10
#define DISTANCE_THRESHOLD 20
#define MEASUREMENT_INTERVAL 1000000

volatile uint32_t rising_edge_timestamp = 0;
volatile uint32_t falling_edge_timestamp = 0;

void handle_echo_pulse(int gpio, int level, uint32_t tick)
{
    if (level == 1)
    {
        rising_edge_timestamp = tick;
    }
    else
    {
        falling_edge_timestamp = tick;
    }
}

void handle_sigint(int signum)
{
    gpioTerminate();
    exit(EXIT_SUCCESS);
}

int main(void)
{
    if (gpioInitialise() < 0)
    {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to initialise pigpio\n");
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    gpioSetMode(TRIGGER_PIN, PI_OUTPUT);
    gpioSetMode(ECHO_PIN, PI_INPUT);
    gpioSetMode(BUZZER_PIN, PI_OUTPUT);

    gpioSetAlertFuncEx(ECHO_PIN, handle_echo_pulse);

    signal(SIGINT, handle_sigint);

    while (1)
    {
        gpioWrite(TRIGGER_PIN, PI_ON);
        gpioDelay(TRIGGER_PULSE_WIDTH);
        gpioWrite(TRIGGER_PIN, PI_OFF);

        gpioDelay(MEASUREMENT_INTERVAL);

        if (falling_edge_timestamp > rising_edge_timestamp)
        {
            uint32_t pulse_width = falling_edge_timestamp - rising_edge_timestamp;
            double distance = pulse_width * 0.0343 / 2;
            printf("Distance: %.2f cm\n", distance);

            if (distance < DISTANCE_THRESHOLD)
            {
                gpioWrite(BUZZER_PIN, PI_ON);
            }
            else
            {
                gpioWrite(BUZZER_PIN, PI_OFF);
            }
        }
    }

    return EXIT_SUCCESS;
}

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to implement a parking assist system with an HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor (trigger on GPIO4, echo on GPIO17) and an SG90 servo motor (signal on GPIO18). Measure distance and display it in centimeters on the console, and rotate the servo proportionally to distance: 0 degrees (500 us pulse) at 200 cm, 90 degrees (1500 us pulse) at 110 cm, and 180 degrees (2500 us pulse) at 20 cm. Use gpioDelay for timing rather than busy-wait loops. Check pigpio initialisation, handle echo timeout by returning -1.0, and retry on sensor errors. Update the distance reading and servo angle every 100 ms, running continuously until interrupted. Handle SIGINT with a graceful cleanup: stop the servo, terminate pigpio, and exit cleanly.

Use a 10 us trigger pulse (not 10 ms), and measure the echo pulse width with microsecond precision using gpioTick(), applying a 50 ms (50000 us) timeout on both the rising and falling edges and returning -1.0 on timeout. Initialise pigpio with error checking, exiting with a clear message on failure; check every pigpio call, handle sensor timeout, and avoid division by zero or invalid angles. Handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) by stopping the servo (gpioServo with 0) and terminating pigpio cleanly. Use only pigpio, not wiringPi.

#include <stdio.h>

#include <pigpio.h>

#define MPU6050_I2C_ADDR 0x68

#define MPU6050_CONFIG 0x1A

Use the high-repeatability measurement command 0xFD, which returns 6 bytes: 2 bytes temperature MSB+LSB, 1 CRC byte, 2 bytes humidity MSB+LSB, 1 CRC byte; wait at least 10 ms for the measurement to complete before reading. prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to interface with a Sensirion SCD40 CO2 sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x62 (standard 100 kHz clock-stretching compatible settings), for monitoring indoor air quality in a smart ventilation system. Send the Start Periodic Measurement command (0x21B1) and wait at least 1 second before the first read attempt. Poll the data-ready flag (0xE4B8) before reading measurements, and only read data (0xEC05) once the flag indicates data is ready; read 9 bytes (6 data bytes plus 3 CRC bytes) and verify the CRC-8 checksum for each 2-byte word (polynomial 0x31, initialization 0xFF). CO2 in ppm is the raw value directly; convert temperature as -45 + 175 * raw/(2^16-1) and humidity as 100 * raw/(2^16-1). Note that the SCD40 requires ambient light for its photoacoustic measurement to function correctly. Every 5 seconds, log CO2, temperature, and humidity to 'air_quality.log' as CSV: timestamp,CO2_ppm,Temperature_C,Humidity_pct, flushing immediately. Check every return value from pigpio initialisation, I2C open, and command send; if any step or the CRC check fails, print a descriptive stderr message and retry or exit appropriately. On SIGINT (Ctrl+C), send the Stop Periodic Measurement command (0x3F86), close the I2C handle, terminate pigpio, close the log file, and exit cleanly.

The TMP05 outputs a PWM-style signal where the ratio of high-time to total-cycle-time encodes the temperature; measure the high pulse width (TH) and total cycle width (TL) via busy-wait polling with microsecond-level timing, using gpioTick() for timestamps. Convert the reading to degrees Celsius using Temperature = 4215 - (2143 * TH / TL). Log each valid reading with an ISO-8601 timestamp to 'temperature_log.txt' in append mode, sampling once every 5 seconds. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for clean shutdown, closing the file and releasing pigpio.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to read temperature and humidity from a Sensirion SHT35-DIS-B sensor connected to I2C bus 1 at address 0x44 (ADDR pin tied to GND). Use the single-shot high-repeatability clock-stretching-disabled measurement command (0x2400); after sending it, wait at least 15 ms before reading 6 bytes (temperature MSB, temperature LSB, temperature CRC, humidity MSB, humidity LSB, humidity CRC), validating both CRC-8 checksums (polynomial 0x31, initial value 0xFF). Convert raw values using T = -45 + 175 * raw / 65535 and RH = 100 * raw / 65535. Log each reading with an ISO-8601 timestamp to a CSV file named 'environment.csv' (columns: timestamp,temperature_c,humidity_pct), writing a header row if the file does not already exist or is empty, sampling every 5 seconds. Check pigpio initialisation, I2C open, every I2C read/write, CRC validation, and file open; on failure print a descriptive error to stderr and continue or exit appropriately. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler for clean shutdown that closes the I2C handle and calls gpioTerminate().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the Linux i2c-dev kernel interface (open(), ioctl(), read(), write()) to periodically read temperature and humidity from an Adafruit Si7021 sensor at I2C address 0x40 on bus 1 (GPIO 2/3), simulating a greenhouse monitoring system. Use the Si7021's No Hold Master measurement commands (0xF5 for humidity, 0xF3 for temperature), polling with read attempts until data is available or a 100 ms timeout is reached; read 3 bytes (MSB, LSB, CRC) for each measurement and verify the CRC-8 checksum (polynomial 0x31, initial value 0x00). Use the paired-reading command 0xE0 to read the temperature associated with the previous humidity measurement. Convert raw values using Temperature = 175.72 * raw / 65536.0 - 46.85 and Humidity = 125.0 * raw / 65536.0 - 6.0. Every 5 seconds, log to a CSV file named 'environment.log' with the header 'timestamp,temperature_C,humidity_percent' using ISO-8601 timestamps; on an I2C or CRC error, log a line with 'ERROR' in place of the values and print a descriptive message to stderr, but continue running. Check every system call return value, handle sensor-absent (I2C open failure or NACK) and bus-error paths, and if a read fails, reset the sensor by writing the reset command (0xFE) before the next cycle. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler to cleanly close the I2C file descriptor and exit gracefully.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to read differential pressure and temperature from a Sensirion SDP810-500Pa sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x25, for a simplified HVAC airflow monitoring system. Use the continuous measurement command 0x362F, wait the specified conversion time, then read 9 bytes: pressure MSB, pressure LSB, CRC, temperature MSB, temperature LSB, CRC, and 3 scale factor bytes, validating CRC-8 for both the pressure and temperature raw values. Convert pressure using pressure = raw_pressure / scale_factor - 1000 (Pa), and temperature using temperature = raw_temperature / 200.0 - 45.0 (°C). Sample once per second and log each sample to 'airflow.dat' in binary format, with pressure and temperature each written as a float, keeping the file handle open across samples rather than reopening it on every write. Check pigpio initialisation, I2C open, command write, and read results, and handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths. Use signal handling (SIGINT, SIGTERM) for a graceful shutdown, closing the I2C handle, terminating pigpio, and closing the file on all exit paths.

The sensor operates on the heat transfer principle and returns a 16-bit word whose 2 most significant bits are status bits; mask them off and shift the result right by 2 to obtain the 14-bit raw flow reading. prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to periodically read differential pressure from a Sensirion SDP32 (±125 Pa) sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x21. Send the continuous-measurement command bytes 0x36, 0x2F to start the sensor, then poll 9 bytes per reading: pressure MSB, pressure LSB, pressure CRC, temperature MSB, temperature LSB, temperature CRC, scale-factor MSB, scale-factor LSB, and scale-factor CRC. Verify the CRC-8 checksum on the pressure, temperature, and scale-factor words, and convert the raw pressure using pressure_pa = raw_pressure / scale_factor. Log each timestamped reading to the console at a default sampling interval of 1000 ms, configurable via a command-line argument. Implement robust error handling for I2C communication failures, including sensor-absent and bus-error paths; if the sensor is not physically connected, detect the I2C read/write failures and exit with a clear diagnostic message rather than crashing. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths through signal handling, and make sure the program compiles and runs cleanly in a mocked or emulated environment, exiting with code 0 when terminated by SIGINT or SIGTERM.

#include <stdint.h>
#include <pigpio.h>

#define SDP32_I2C_ADDR 0x21
#define SDP32_I2C_BUS 1
#define SDP32_CMD_START_MEASUREMENT 0x362F
#define SDP32_CMD_STOP_MEASUREMENT 0x3F2F
#define SDP32_CMD_READ_MEASUREMENT 0x0000
#define SDP32_CMD_READ_SCALE_FACTOR 0x3383

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <stdint.h>
#include <pigpio.h>
#include <time.h>
#include <signal.h>
#include <unistd.h>

#define SHT40_ADDR 0x44
#define SHT40_CMD 0xFD
#define SHT40_DATA_LEN 6
#define SHT40_CRC_LEN 1
#define SHT40_CRC_POLY 0x31
#define SHT40_CRC_INIT 0xFF

#define TEMP_OFFSET -45.0
#define TEMP_SCALE 175.0
#define HUM_OFFSET -6.0
#define HUM_SCALE 125.0

#define LOG_FILE "environmental_data.txt"

#define SLEEP_TIME 5

#define CRC8_TABLE_SIZE 256

static uint8_t crc8_table[CRC8_TABLE_SIZE];

static int i2c_handle = -1;
static FILE *log_file = NULL;

static void init_crc8_table(void)
{
    uint8_t i, j;
    uint8_t crc;

    for (i = 0; i < CRC8_TABLE_SIZE; i++) {
        crc = i;
        for (j = 0; j < 8; j++) {
            if (crc & 0x80) {
                crc = (crc << 1) ^ SHT40_CRC_POLY;
            } else {
                crc = crc << 1;
            }
        }
        crc8_table[i] = crc;
    }
}

static uint8_t crc8(uint8_t *data, size_t len)
{
    uint8_t crc = SHT40_CRC_INIT;
    size_t i;

    for (i = 0; i < len; i++) {
        crc = crc8_table[crc ^ data[i]];
    }

    return crc;
}

static void sigint_handler(int signum)
{
    if (i2c_handle >= 0) {
        i2cClose(i2c_handle);
    }
    if (log_file != NULL) {
        fclose(log_file);
    }
    gpioTerminate();
    exit(0);
}

int main(void)
{
    uint8_t data[SHT40_DATA_LEN + SHT40_CRC_LEN];
    uint8_t temp_crc, hum_crc;
    float temp, hum;
    time_t now;
    struct tm *tm;
    char time_str[32];

    if (gpioInitialise() < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "pigpio initialization failed\n");
        return 1;
    }

    i2c_handle = i2cOpen(1, SHT40_ADDR, 0);
    if (i2c_handle < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "failed to open I2C bus\n");
        gpioTerminate();
        return 1;
    }

    log_file = fopen(LOG_FILE, "a");
    if (log_file == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "failed to open log file\n");
        i2cClose(i2c_handle);
        gpioTerminate();
        return 1;
    }

    init_crc8_table();

    signal(SIGINT, sigint_handler);

    while (1) {
        if (i2cWriteByte(i2c_handle, SHT40_CMD) < 0) {
            fprintf(stderr, "failed to write command\n");
            break;
        }

        sleep(1);

        if (i2cReadI2C(i2c_handle, data, SHT40_DATA_LEN + SHT40_CRC_LEN) < 0) {
            fprintf(stderr, "failed to read data\n");
            break;
        }

        temp_crc = crc8(data, SHT40_DATA_LEN / 2);
        hum_crc = crc8(data + SHT40_DATA_LEN / 2, SHT40_DATA_LEN / 2);

        if (temp_crc != data[SHT40_DATA_LEN / 2] || hum_crc != data[SHT40_DATA_LEN / 2 + SHT40_CRC_LEN]) {
            fprintf(stderr, "CRC mismatch\n");
            break;
        }

        temp = TEMP_OFFSET + TEMP_SCALE * ((float) (data[0] << 8 | data[1]) / 65535.0);
        hum = HUM_OFFSET + HUM_SCALE * ((float) (data[2] << 8 | data[3]) / 65535.0);

        now = time(NULL);
        tm = localtime(&now);
        strftime(time_str, sizeof(time_str), "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S", tm);

        fprintf(log_file, "%s, %.2f, %.2f\n", time_str, temp, hum);
        fflush(log_file);

        sleep(SLEEP_TIME);
    }

    if (i2c_handle >= 0) {
        i2cClose(i2c_handle);
    }
    if (log_file != NULL) {
        fclose(log_file);
    }
    gpioTerminate();

    return 0;
}

prompt: Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library (never wiringPi) to periodically sample temperature from a Texas Instruments TMP117 high-accuracy sensor over I2C bus 1 at its default address 0x48. Read the 2-byte big-endian temperature register 0x00 every 5 seconds and convert it using the 0.0078125 °C LSB resolution. Store readings in a rolling circular buffer in memory and persist the entire buffer to a binary file named temperature_log.dat on every sample and on exit. Check that pigpio initialization and I2C handle creation succeed. If a read fails, log the error, skip that sample, and continue running rather than crashing. Implement graceful shutdown on SIGINT/SIGTERM that flushes the buffer to the file and releases all resources — the I2C handle and pigpio — on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses pigpio to read temperature and humidity from a Sensirion SHTC3 sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x70, for an indoor air quality monitoring system. The SHTC3 operates at 1.8 V but tolerates 3.3 V on SDA/SCL; wire VDD to 3.3 V (Pin 1), VSS to GND (Pin 2), SDA to GPIO 2 (Pin 3), and SCL to GPIO 3 (Pin 4). Issue the normal-power measurement command 0x7866 (clock stretching disabled), wait at least 12.4 ms for the conversion, then read 6 bytes: temperature MSB, temperature LSB, temperature CRC8, humidity MSB, humidity LSB, humidity CRC8. Validate each pair with CRC-8 (polynomial 0x31, initial value 0xFF), then convert using T = 175 * raw / 65535 - 45 and RH = 100 * raw / 65535, rejecting readings outside -40 to 125 °C or 0 to 100 %RH. Log valid readings every 5 seconds to shtc3_environment.log in the format "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS,Temperature(C),Humidity(%)" with two decimal places, printing valid readings to stdout and errors to stderr. Handle I2C write/read errors, CRC failures, out-of-range values, and file-open errors gracefully without crashing. On SIGINT, close the I2C handle, call gpioTerminate(), and exit cleanly.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to interface with a Silicon Labs Si7202 I2C Hall-effect sensor at address 0x40 on I2C bus 1, for a precise rotational speed measurement system. Handle errors from I2C initialization, sensor communication, and file I/O; if a sensor read fails, log an entry with NaN values and continue running.
