Every 2 seconds, read the RAW pressure register at 0x0A2C (2 bytes, big-endian) and the RAW temperature register at 0x0A2E (2 bytes, big-endian), and log the results with an ISO-8601 timestamp to pressure_log.txt. Convert raw pressure to kPa using pressure_kPa = (raw - output_min) * (pmax_kPa - pmin_kPa) / (output_max - output_min), with output_min=0, output_max=32768, pmin=0 kPa, pmax=800 kPa; convert raw temperature using temp_C = raw * 0.01 - 40. Check every pigpio and I2C call; if a read fails, log the error with a timestamp rather than skipping silently, and continue running. Run the program indefinitely until interrupted, performing clean resource release on all exit paths, including SIGINT and SIGTERM: close the I2C handle, close the log file, and call gpioTerminate().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library for both I2C and GPIO (not wiringPi) to interface with an STMicroelectronics LM75B temperature sensor on I2C bus 1 at address 0x48. Every 1 second, read the 2-byte temperature register 0x00 and convert it using the LM75B's signed 9-bit format (0.5 °C resolution, using bits D9-D1, with D0 always 0). Store each reading in a 60-element circular buffer in memory and compute the running average. Control a cooling fan on GPIO 18 (BCM numbering) with hysteresis: turn it on when the running average exceeds 28.0 °C and off when it falls below 26.0 °C. Check pigpio initialization, the I2C bus open, every I2C read, and every GPIO write; log failures to stderr and retry on the next cycle without crashing. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown: stop the fan, close the I2C handle, and terminate pigpio cleanly.
raw:
```c
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <signal.h>
#include <pigpio.h>

#define I2C_BUS 1
#define I2C_ADDR 0x48
#define I2C_REG 0x00
#define GPIO_PIN 18
#define BUFFER_SIZE 60
#define HYS_ON 28.0
#define HYS_OFF 26.0

int running = 1;

void sig_handler(int signo) {
    if (signo == SIGINT || signo == SIGTERM) {
        running = 0;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int handle, ret, i;
    uint8_t data[2];
    float temp, avg, buffer[BUFFER_SIZE];

    // Initialize pigpio
    if (gpioInitialise() < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to initialize pigpio\n");
        return 1;
    }

    // Open I2C bus
    handle = i2cOpen(I2C_BUS, I2C_ADDR, 0);
    if (handle < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to open I2C bus\n");
        gpioTerminate();
        return 1;
    }

    // Set up GPIO pin
    ret = gpioSetMode(GPIO_PIN, PI_OUTPUT);
    if (ret != 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to set GPIO pin mode\n");
        i2cClose(handle);
        gpioTerminate();
        return 1;
    }

    // Set up signal handler
    signal(SIGINT, sig_handler);
    signal(SIGTERM, sig_handler);

    // Main loop
    while (running) {
        // Read temperature register
        ret = i2cReadI2CBlockData(handle, I2C_REG, data, 2);
        if (ret != 2) {
            fprintf(stderr, "Failed to read I2C register\n");
            i2cClose(handle);
            gpioTerminate();
            return 1;
        }

        // Convert temperature
        temp = (data[0] << 1) | (data[1] >> 7);
        if (temp & 0x100) {
            temp -= 0x200;
        }
        temp *= 0.5;

        // Add to buffer and compute average
        buffer[i] = temp;
        i = (i + 1) % BUFFER_SIZE;
        avg = 0;
        for (int j = 0; j < BUFFER_SIZE; j++) {
            avg += buffer[j];
        }
        avg /= BUFFER_SIZE;

        // Control fan
        if (avg > HYS_ON) {
            ret = gpioWrite(GPIO_PIN, 1);
            if (ret != 0) {
                fprintf(stderr, "Failed to write GPIO pin\n");
                i2cClose(handle);
                gpioTerminate();
                return 1;
            }
        } else if (avg < HYS_OFF) {
            ret = gpioWrite(GPIO_PIN, 0);
            if (ret != 0) {
                fprintf(stderr, "Failed to write GPIO pin\n");
                i2cClose(handle);
                gpioTerminate();
                return 1;
            }
        }

        // Sleep for 1 second
        sleep(1);
    }

    // Clean up
    i2cClose(handle);
    gpioTerminate();

    return 0;
}

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library for I2C communication to read differential pressure and temperature from a Sensirion SDP800-500Pa sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x25. Send the continuous-measurement command 0x362F, wait at least 45 ms, then read 9 bytes: 2 bytes differential pressure plus 1 CRC byte, 2 bytes temperature plus 1 CRC byte, and 3 bytes of scale-factor data. Validate CRC-8 (polynomial 0x31, initial value 0xFF) for the pressure and temperature readings. Convert the raw differential pressure by dividing by the scale factor, taken as a signed integer from the last 16 bits of the read data, and convert the raw temperature by dividing by 200. Log each reading with a timestamp to flow_data.txt. Handle I2C communication errors and sensor-absent scenarios gracefully. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths using SIGINT signal handling.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library (not wiringPi) to read temperature and humidity from an Adafruit Si7021 sensor over I2C bus 1 (GPIO 2/3 for SDA/SCL) at address 0x40. Use i2cReadDevice/i2cWriteDevice for raw byte transfers, since the Si7021 protocol uses single-byte commands followed by 2-byte reads rather than register-addressed access: issue 'Measure Relative Humidity, No Master Hold' (0xF5) and 'Measure Temperature, No Master Hold' (0xF3), or read temperature from the previous RH measurement via command 0xE0, waiting at least 20 ms after a no-hold command before reading the result. Retry each I2C transaction up to 3 times on failure. Convert raw values using Temperature = 175.72 * raw / 65536 - 46.85 and Humidity = 125 * raw / 65536 - 6, clamped to 0-100%. Sample every 60 seconds and log each reading with an ISO-8601 timestamp, in CSV format timestamp,temperature_c,humidity_pct, to environment.log (flushing after every write) and to stdout. Log errors with timestamps to both the log file and stderr. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for clean shutdown, closing the I2C handle and calling gpioTerminate().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to read temperature and humidity from a TI HDC1080 sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x40, initializing pigpio and opening the I2C bus with error checking. Open the I2C adapter with open() and set the slave address via ioctl(I2C_SLAVE). Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to interface with a Sensirion SCD40 CO2 sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x62. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library (NOT wiringPi) to read differential pressure from a Sensirion SDP810-500Pa sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x25, for a basic HVAC airflow monitoring application. Poll MEASUREMENT_CONFIG until bit 0 clears, or time out after about 500 ms, before reading temperature from registers 0x00-0x01 and humidity from registers 0x02-0x03. Convert using temperature = raw/65536*165 - 40 and humidity = raw/65536*100. Check every pigpio call, detect sensor-absent (NAK) and bus-error paths, and enforce a maximum retry count for transient I2C failures. prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that implements a PID-controlled reflow oven using a MAX6675 thermocouple over SPI0 (CE0/CE1) and a solid-state relay on GPIO17, reading a target temperature profile from profile.txt (lines of time_seconds,target_temp_celsius). Use libgpiod for GPIO control and spidev for SPI communication. The MAX6675 returns a 16-bit word where bit 2 is the open-circuit flag and bits 3-14 hold the 12-bit temperature; read it at 1 Hz. The PID controller's output, from 0.0 to 1.0, sets the solid-state relay's duty cycle over each 1-second period. Log temperature data to reflow_log.csv. Implement robust error handling for SPI communication and GPIO control, including sensor-absent and bus-error paths, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths through signal handling.

Use the libgpiod library for chip-select line management and the standard Linux spidev interface for SPI communication (do not use wiringPi). Initialize the MAX31865 for 3-wire RTD mode with bias voltage enabled, read the RTD registers, check the fault status register, and calculate temperature using the Callendar-Van Dusen equation. Implement robust error handling for SPI communication failures and sensor read errors, handling sensor-absent and SPI bus-error paths by logging errors without crashing. Implement graceful shutdown on SIGINT/SIGTERM, properly closing the SPI device file descriptor and the log file.

Read the 16-bit temperature register (0x00) every 1 second; the value arrives two's-complement, MSB first, left-shifted by 5 bits (bits [15:5] hold the temperature, bits [4:0] are always 0), so divide the signed 16-bit value by 256.0 to get degrees Celsius. Log each reading to an in-memory circular buffer with a capacity of 60 samples and compute the running average. Trigger an LED on GPIO 18 (BCM numbering) if the temperature exceeds 28.0°C, turning it off otherwise. Use a background thread with a mutex-protected circular buffer for data acquisition. Check every I2C read/write and GPIO init call, handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths by logging to stderr and attempting re-initialization, and ensure clean resource release — close the I2C file descriptor, release the GPIO lines, destroy the mutex — on all exit paths including SIGINT.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that regulates a resistive heater connected through a logic-level MOSFET on GPIO18 (hardware PWM) using the pigpio library (not wiringPi). Measure temperature with a PT100 RTD through a MAX31865 RTD-to-digital converter over SPI0 (CE0, SPI mode 1, 500 kHz), using a 430-ohm reference resistor for the PT100 (nominal resistance 100 ohms). Initialize the MAX31865 by writing 0xC1 to the configuration register (0x80) to enable VBIAS, enable auto-conversion, and clear faults. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM gracefully — turn off the heater, close SPI, terminate pigpio, exit cleanly. prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to create a mood light that adjusts a common-anode RGB LED based on CPU temperature read from /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp every 0.5 seconds. Red, Green, and Blue cathodes connect to GPIO 17, 18, and 27 (BCM), with the common anode on 3.3 V and current-limiting resistors on each cathode line. Use hardware PWM via gpioPWM (range 0-255) on each pin; since the LED is common-anode, a channel is fully off at duty 255 and fully on at duty 0, so invert the desired brightness accordingly. Apply temperature thresholds from the millidegree sysfs value: below 40000 m°C, solid Blue (R=0,G=0,B=255); 40000-59999 m°C, solid Green (R=0,G=255,B=0); 60000 m°C and above, solid Red (R=255,G=0,B=0). Print the current temperature (m°C) and RGB values to stdout each cycle. Check the return value of gpioInitialise(); on failure, print an error to stderr and exit with non-zero status. When reading the temperature file, handle both fopen failure and short or failed reads (check ferror); on any read error, print a diagnostic to stderr and skip the update cycle rather than using a bogus value, and close the file handle on every code path. Install a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM, using a volatile sig_atomic_t flag and performing cleanup in main's exit path rather than inside the handler, so that Ctrl+C cleanly turns off all three channels (PWM duty 255 for common-anode off) and calls gpioTerminate() before exiting. Run an infinite loop until interrupted.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ to read humidity and temperature from a DHT22 sensor connected to GPIO4 (BCM numbering, physical pin 7), using the pigpio library for bit-banging the 1-wire protocol and libcurl for HTTP POST requests. Send a start signal by pulling the data line low for at least 1 ms, then read the 40-bit response. Parse the data, validate the 8-bit checksum, and POST the readings as a JSON payload to http://yourserver.com/api/humidity. Handle sensor-absent, checksum, and network errors gracefully with up to 3 retries. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including signal handling for SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Use a falling-edge ISR on GPIO4 with an internal pull-up to toggle logging on and off, debouncing in the ISR using pigpio tick comparison (at least 200000 us). Read the BMP180 calibration coefficients from registers 0xAA-0xBE at startup and validate them, failing cleanly if the sensor is absent or returns invalid data. Use oversampling OSS=3 for pressure measurements with the correct 26 ms conversion delay, and implement the full Bosch BMP180 compensation algorithm using integer arithmetic, with no floating-point pow calls. Log only when logging is enabled; when disabled, print a status message. Sample every 2 seconds. Handle SIGINT cleanly by closing the I2C handle and releasing pigpio resources before exiting. Include a command-line option -s <url> to override the default server URL. prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 using the libgpiod API (not sysfs or wiringPi) to sample the analog audio output of an Adafruit MAX9814 Electret Microphone Amplifier. Connect the MAX9814 OUT pin to GPIO 17 (configured as input) and the GAIN pin to GPIO 18 (configured as output), setting GPIO 18 LOW to select 60dB gain. Since the MAX9814 provides an analog signal, rapidly poll the digital input pin, at a 10 ms interval, to detect rising edges (logic HIGH) as peak sound events. Log each detected peak to audio_log.txt with a timestamp formatted as 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS LEVEL', where LEVEL is 1 for a rising edge. Handle all libgpiod initialization and I/O errors robustly, checking the return value of every API call, and ensure clean release of all libgpiod resources on all exit paths via SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling. Print a startup message and run indefinitely until interrupted.
raw:
```
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <time.h>
#include <signal.h>
#include <libgpiod.h>

#define MAX9814_GAIN_PIN 18
#define MAX9814_OUT_PIN 17

#define LOG_FILE "audio_log.txt"

struct gpiod_chip *chip;
struct gpiod_line *gain_line;
struct gpiod_line *out_line;

void signal_handler(int sig) {
    printf("Exiting...\n");
    gpiod_line_release(gain_line);
    gpiod_line_release(out_line);
    gpiod_chip_close(chip);
    exit(0);
}

int main(int argc, char *argv[]) {
    struct timespec ts;
    struct tm *tm;
    char timestamp[20];
    int level;

    // Initialize libgpiod
    chip = gpiod_chip_open_by_name("gpiochip0");
    if (!chip) {
        printf("Error opening gpiochip0\n");
        return 1;
    }

    // Configure MAX9814 gain pin as output
    gain_line = gpiod_chip_get_line(chip, MAX9814_GAIN_PIN);
    if (!gain_line) {
        printf("Error getting line %d\n", MAX9814_GAIN_PIN);
        return 1;
    }
    if (gpiod_line_request_output(gain_line, "gain", 0) < 0) {
        printf("Error requesting output for line %d\n", MAX9814_GAIN_PIN);
        return 1;
    }

    // Configure MAX9814 out pin as input
    out_line = gpiod_chip_get_line(chip, MAX9814_OUT_PIN);
    if (!out_line) {
        printf("Error getting line %d\n", MAX9814_OUT_PIN);
        return 1;
    }
    if (gpiod_line_request_input(out_line, "out") < 0) {
        printf("Error requesting input for line %d\n", MAX9814_OUT_PIN);
        return 1;
    }

    // Set gain to 60dB
    if (gpiod_line_set_value(gain_line, 0) < 0) {
        printf("Error setting value for line %d\n", MAX9814_GAIN_PIN);
        return 1;
    }

    // Open log file
    FILE *log_file = fopen(LOG_FILE, "a");
    if (!log_file) {
        printf("Error opening log file\n");
        return 1;
    }

    // Register signal handler
    signal(SIGINT, signal_handler);
    signal(SIGTERM, signal_handler);

    // Main loop
    while (1) {
        // Poll MAX9814 out pin for rising edges
        if (gpiod_line_event_wait(out_line, -1) < 0) {
            printf("Error waiting for event on line %d\n", MAX9814_OUT_PIN);
            return 1;
        }
        if (gpiod_line_event_read(out_line) == GPIOD_LINE_EVENT_RISING_EDGE) {
            // Get current timestamp
            clock_gettime(CLOCK_REALTIME, &ts);
            tm = localtime(&ts.tv_sec);
            strftime(timestamp, sizeof(timestamp), "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S", tm);

            // Log timestamp and level
            level = gpiod_line_get_value(out_line);
            fprintf(log_file, "%s %d\n", timestamp, level);
            fflush(log_file);
        }
    }

    return 0;
}

It then configures the out pin as an input and polls it for rising edges. When a rising edge is detected, the program gets the current timestamp, logs it along with the level (1) to the log file, and flushes the log file. The program registers a signal handler to handle SIGINT and SIGTERM signals, and releases all libgpiod resources on exit.

This program assumes that the MAX9814 is connected to GPIO 17 (out pin) and GPIO 18 (gain pin) on the Raspberry Pi. It also assumes that the log file audio_log.txt exists and is writable.

Every 5 seconds, log a timestamped line with the IAQ, TVOC, and eCO2 values to 'air_quality_log.csv'. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 using the libgpiod v1 API to monitor a SainSmart TTP223B capacitive touch sensor connected to GPIO 17 (physical pin 11, active-high): the sensor outputs HIGH while touched and LOW when released. Open gpiochip0 by name and request the line as input with the consumer label "ttp223_tamper". Poll the line every 100 ms using CLOCK_MONOTONIC. If the sensor remains continuously touched for more than 5 seconds, print an intrusion alert to stdout once per touch event (not repeatedly), and reset the timer when the sensor is released. Check every libgpiod call for failure and print strerror(errno) on error; if a sensor read fails mid-loop, print an error and exit with EXIT_FAILURE after cleanup. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, releasing the line and closing the chip on all exit paths. Do not use sysfs or wiringPi.

During initialization, verify the sensor's PART ID (0x45), write 0x17 to the HW_KEY register, configure the CHLIST register (0x01) to enable UV and ALS_VIS, and use the ALS_FORCE command (0x06) to trigger measurements. Every 1 second, continuously read UV index and Visible ALS data, print the readings to the console, and log them to a CSV file named 'uv_als_log.csv' with columns timestamp, uv_index, als_visible. Handle potential I2C errors and sensor-absent/bus-error paths gracefully. Implement clean resource release on all exit paths, including signal handling for SIGINT and SIGTERM.

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <pigpio.h>
#include <time.h>

#define SENSOR_ADDR 0x60
#define SENSOR_PART_ID 0x45
#define SENSOR_HW_KEY 0x07
#define SENSOR_CHLIST 0x01
#define SENSOR_ALS_FORCE 0x06
#define SENSOR_ALS_VIS_DATA 0x22
#define SENSOR_UV_DATA 0x2C

#define SENSOR_PART_ID_VAL 0x45
#define SENSOR_HW_KEY_VAL 0x17
#define SENSOR_CHLIST_VAL 0x03

#define SENSOR_ALS_FORCE_VAL 0x01

#define SENSOR_ALS_VIS_DATA_VAL 0x00
#define SENSOR_UV_DATA_VAL 0x00

#define SENSOR_ALS_VIS_DATA_LEN 2
#define SENSOR_UV_DATA_LEN 2

#define SENSOR_TIMEOUT 1000

#define CSV_FILE "uv_als_log.csv"

int main(int argc, char *argv[])
{
    int handle;
    int ret;
    int uv_index;
    int als_visible;
    time_t timestamp;
    FILE *csv_file;

    if (gpioInitialise() < 0)
    {
        fprintf(stderr, "pigpio initialisation failed\n");
        return 1;
    }

    handle = i2cOpen(1, SENSOR_ADDR, 0);
    if (handle < 0)
    {
        fprintf(stderr, "i2cOpen failed\n");
        gpioTerminate();
        return 1;
    }

    ret = i2cWriteByteData(handle, SENSOR_HW_KEY, SENSOR_HW_KEY_VAL);
    if (ret < 0)
    {
        fprintf(stderr, "i2cWriteByteData failed\n");
        i2cClose(handle);
        gpioTerminate();
        return 1;
    }

    ret = i2cWriteByteData(handle, SENSOR_CHLIST, SENSOR_CHLIST_VAL);
    if (ret < 0)
    {
        fprintf(stderr, "i2cWriteByteData failed\n");
        i2cClose(handle);
        gpioTerminate();
        return 1;
    }

    ret = i2cWriteByteData(handle, SENSOR_ALS_FORCE, SENSOR_ALS_FORCE_VAL);
    if (ret < 0)
    {
        fprintf(stderr, "i2cWriteByteData failed\n");
        i2cClose(handle);
        gpioTerminate();
        return 1;
    }

    csv_file = fopen(CSV_FILE, "w");
    if (csv_file == NULL)
    {
        fprintf(stderr, "fopen failed\n");
        i2cClose(handle);
        gpioTerminate();
        return 1;
    }

    fprintf(csv_file, "timestamp,uv_index,als_visible\n");

    while (1)
    {
        ret = i2cReadI2CBlockData(handle, SENSOR_UV_DATA, SENSOR_UV_DATA_LEN, (char *)&uv_index);
        if (ret < 0)
        {
            fprintf(stderr, "i2cReadI2CBlockData failed\n");
            break;
        }

        ret = i2cReadI2CBlockData(handle, SENSOR_ALS_VIS_DATA, SENSOR_ALS_VIS_DATA_LEN, (char *)&als_visible);
        if (ret < 0)
        {
            fprintf(stderr, "i2cReadI2CBlockData failed\n");
            break;
        }

        timestamp = time(NULL);

        fprintf(csv_file, "%ld,%d,%d\n", timestamp, uv_index, als_visible);

        gpioDelay(1000000);
    }

    fclose(csv_file);
    i2cClose(handle);
    gpioTerminate();

    return 0;
}

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 to read flow rates from two Sensirion SLF3S-0600F Liquid Flow Sensors on I2C at addresses 0x36 and 0x37, using the Linux I2C character-device API (open()/ioctl() on /dev/i2c-1) for I2C communication and the libgpiod library for GPIO control. Initialize each sensor by sending the start-measurement command 0x3608 to I2C command register 0x08 and wait 100 ms for the first measurement. Read 9 bytes from register 0x00 (three 3-byte measurements: flow, temperature, CRC), validating each flow measurement with the Sensirion 8-bit CRC (polynomial 0x31, initial value 0xFF); on an I2C error or CRC failure, log the error and skip that sensor's reading for the cycle. Convert the raw 16-bit signed flow value to ml/min using a scale factor of 0.036. Every 1 second, log the average flow rate of the two sensors to 'flow_log.txt', and drive an alarm on GPIO 17 high when that average is below 0.5 ml/min and low otherwise. Implement clean shutdown on SIGINT/SIGTERM: release the GPIO lines, close the I2C file descriptors, and close the log file. Loop continuously with a 1-second interval between reads.

Poll both sensors every 100 ms. Turn the LED ON immediately when either sensor reads LOW, and turn it OFF when both read HIGH. Verify pigpio initialization, validate every gpioSetMode/gpioRead/gpioWrite return code, and ensure clean resource release (gpioTerminate) on all exit paths, including SIGINT/SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to monitor a conveyor belt with two E18-D80NK IR obstacle sensors connected to GPIO 17 and GPIO 18, which output LOW (0) when an object is detected and HIGH (1) when clear. A stall is confirmed when both sensors read LOW continuously for at least 2 seconds; on a confirmed stall, log a timestamped entry to 'stall_log.txt', avoiding duplicate log entries for the same stall event. Check pigpio initialization, validate every sensor read, handle file I/O errors, and ensure clean resource release on SIGINT/SIGTERM.

```
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <signal.h>
#include <time.h>
#include <pigpio.h>

#define SENSOR_1 17
#define SENSOR_2 18
#define STALL_TIME 2000000

FILE *fp;

void sig_handler(int signo)
{
    if (signo == SIGINT || signo == SIGTERM)
    {
        printf("Exiting...\n");
        fclose(fp);
        gpioTerminate();
        exit(0);
    }
}

int main(void)
{
    if (gpioInitialise() < 0)
    {
        printf("pigpio initialization failed\n");
        return 1;
    }

    gpioSetMode(SENSOR_1, PI_INPUT);
    gpioSetMode(SENSOR_2, PI_INPUT);

    fp = fopen("stall_log.txt", "a");
    if (fp == NULL)
    {
        printf("Error opening file\n");
        return 1;
    }

    signal(SIGINT, sig_handler);
    signal(SIGTERM, sig_handler);

    int sensor1_prev = 0;
    int sensor2_prev = 0;
    int sensor1_curr = 0;
    int sensor2_curr = 0;
    int stall_detected = 0;
    int stall_start_time = 0;

    while (1)
    {
        sensor1_curr = gpioRead(SENSOR_1);
        sensor2_curr = gpioRead(SENSOR_2);

        if (sensor1_curr == 0 && sensor2_curr == 0)
        {
            if (sensor1_prev == 0 && sensor2_prev == 0)
            {
                if (!stall_detected)
                {
                    stall_detected = 1;
                    stall_start_time = gpioTick();
                }
                else if (gpioTick() - stall_start_time >= STALL_TIME)
                {
                    time_t t = time(NULL);
                    struct tm *tm = localtime(&t);
                    char time_str[64];
                    strftime(time_str, sizeof(time_str), "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S", tm);
                    fprintf(fp, "%s\n", time_str);
                    fflush(fp);
                    stall_detected = 0;
                }
            }
            else
            {
                stall_detected = 0;
            }
        }
        else
        {
            stall_detected = 0;
        }

        sensor1_prev = sensor1_curr;
        sensor2_prev = sensor2_curr;
    }

    fclose(fp);
    gpioTerminate();
    return 0;
}

- If both sensors read LOW, the program checks if a stall has already been detected. If not, it sets the stall_detected flag and records the current time. prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to interface with a Texas Instruments TMAG5170-Q1 I2C 3D Hall-Effect sensor on I2C bus 1 at address 0x0E (A0=A1=0). Configure the sensor for continuous-conversion mode with all three axes enabled and a 50 mT range. Verify the device ID register (0x00, expected value 0x8D) at startup, and write a CSV header row to 'magnetic_log.csv' if the file is newly created. Every 100 ms, read the X, Y, and Z magnetic field readings, convert the raw 16-bit two's-complement values to mT using the appropriate LSB scale factor for the 50 mT range, and log them with ISO-8601 timestamps to 'magnetic_log.csv'. Check every I2C read/write return code, and handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths by logging errors to stderr and continuing. Register a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler for clean resource release (close the I2C handle, close the file, call gpioTerminate). Run an infinite loop until interrupted by Ctrl+C.

Write a robust C daemon for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to monitor a SEN0193 Water Level Sensor (digital output) connected to GPIO 23, using a pull-down resistor on the input to avoid floating states when the sensor is dry. Poll the sensor every 2 seconds. When water is detected (logic HIGH), print an alert message to stdout and append a timestamped entry in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS ALERT: Water detected' to 'flood_log.txt'. Check pigpio initialization, handle GPIO read failures with an automatic re-initialization attempt after 60 seconds (logging error entries to the same log file), and ensure clean resource release on SIGINT/SIGTERM.
raw:
```
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <time.h>
#include <pigpio.h>

#define GPIO_PIN 23
#define LOG_FILE "flood_log.txt"
#define LOG_ENTRY_SIZE 100

int main(int argc, char *argv[])
{
    int rc;
    int gpio_val;
    time_t t;
    struct tm *tm;
    char log_entry[LOG_ENTRY_SIZE];

    if (gpioInitialise() < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "pigpio initialisation failed\n");
        return 1;
    }

    gpioSetMode(GPIO_PIN, PI_INPUT);
    gpioSetPullUpDown(GPIO_PIN, PI_PUD_DOWN);

    while (1) {
        rc = gpioRead(GPIO_PIN);
        if (rc < 0) {
            fprintf(stderr, "gpioRead failed\n");
            sleep(60);
            continue;
        }

        if (rc == PI_HIGH) {
            t = time(NULL);
            tm = localtime(&t);
            strftime(log_entry, LOG_ENTRY_SIZE, "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S ALERT: Water detected\n", tm);
            printf("%s", log_entry);

            FILE *fp = fopen(LOG_FILE, "a");
            if (fp == NULL) {
                fprintf(stderr, "Error opening log file\n");
                return 1;
            }
            fprintf(fp, "%s", log_entry);
            fclose(fp);
        }

        sleep(2);
    }

    gpioTerminate();
    return 0;
}

```
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <time.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <pigpio.h>

#define I2C_BUS 1
#define I2C_ADDR 0x10
#define I2C_CONFIG_REG 0x00
#define I2C_ALS_REG 0x04
#define I2C_CONFIG_VAL 0x0000
#define PWM_GPIO 18
#define PWM_FREQ 1000
#define PWM_RANGE 100
#define LUX_100 100
#define LUX_500 500
#define LUX_1000 1000
#define LUX_SCALE 0.0576

int main(void) {
    FILE *log_file = fopen("grow_log.txt", "w");
    if (log_file == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Error opening log file\n");
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    if (gpioInitialise() < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Error initializing pigpio\n");
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    int i2c_handle = i2cOpen(I2C_BUS, I2C_ADDR, 0);
    if (i2c_handle < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Error opening I2C bus\n");
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    if (i2cWriteWordData(i2c_handle, I2C_CONFIG_REG, I2C_CONFIG_VAL) < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Error writing to I2C config register\n");
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    if (gpioSetPWMfrequency(PWM_GPIO, PWM_FREQ) < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Error setting PWM frequency\n");
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    if (gpioSetPWMrange(PWM_GPIO, PWM_RANGE) < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Error setting PWM range\n");
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    while (1) {
        int lux_raw = i2cReadWordData(i2c_handle, I2C_ALS_REG);
        if (lux_raw < 0) {
            fprintf(stderr, "Error reading from I2C ALS register\n");
            return EXIT_FAILURE;
        }

        double lux = lux_raw * LUX_SCALE;
        int brightness = 0;
        if (lux < LUX_100) {
            brightness = PWM_RANGE;
        } else if (lux < LUX_500) {
            brightness = PWM_RANGE * 3 / 4;
        } else if (lux < LUX_1000) {
            brightness = PWM_RANGE / 2;
        } else {
            brightness = PWM_RANGE / 4;
        }

        if (gpioPWM(PWM_GPIO, brightness) < 0) {
            fprintf(stderr, "Error setting PWM duty cycle\n");
            return EXIT_FAILURE;
        }

        time_t now = time(NULL);
        struct tm *time_info = localtime(&now);
        char timestamp[32];
        strftime(timestamp, sizeof(timestamp), "%FT%T%z", time_info);

        fprintf(log_file, "%s,%.2f,%d\n", timestamp, lux, brightness);
        fflush(log_file);

        sleep(1);
    }

    gpioPWM(PWM_GPIO, 0);
    i2cClose(i2c_handle);
    fclose(log_file);
    gpioTerminate();

    return EXIT_SUCCESS;
}

The program opens the I2C bus, configures the sensor, and sets up the PWM for the LED. It then enters a loop that reads the lux value from the sensor, calculates the brightness based on the lux value, and sets the PWM duty cycle. It also logs the timestamp, lux value, brightness, and error code to the log file. The program handles errors and releases resources on all exit paths. It also handles SIGINT/SIGTERM signals by turning off the LED, closing the I2C bus, closing the log file, and terminating pigpio.

The program uses the following constants:

- I2C_BUS: The I2C bus number (1)
- I2C_ADDR: The I2C address of the sensor (0x10)

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library for a simulated security keypad that interfaces with an 8-channel TTP226 capacitive touch sensor module whose 8 digital output channels are connected to GPIO 2-9 (BCM numbering), and an LED on GPIO 17 that lights whenever any touch is detected. Initialize pigpio and verify success, exiting with an error message on failure; configure GPIO 2-9 as inputs with pull-down resistors and GPIO 17 as an output. Poll the inputs every 50 ms and debounce each channel so a single touch is logged only once per press. Log each new touch event to 'touch_log.txt' in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS - Channel X Touched', where X (1-8) corresponds to GPIO 2-9. Turn the LED on when any channel transitions from untouched to touched, and off when all channels are released. Check all file I/O operations for errors and print diagnostics to stderr. Implement a clean signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM that turns off the LED, releases pigpio resources, and exits gracefully.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to read ambient light data from a Texas Instruments OPT3001 sensor for a smart greenhouse environment monitoring system. Use I2C bus 1 (/dev/i2c-1, pigpio bus 1), OPT3001 address 0x44, configuration register 0x01, and result register 0x00. prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the libgpiod character-device API (gpiod_chip_open_by_name, gpiod_chip_get_line, gpiod_line_request_input, gpiod_line_request_output, gpiod_line_get_value, gpiod_line_set_value on device 'gpiochip0'; not wiringPi or sysfs) to implement a flame-detection safety system with a Keyes KY-026 flame sensor and an active buzzer. The KY-026 digital-output pin is connected to GPIO17 (physical pin 11) and is active-low: it reads LOW when a flame is detected and HIGH otherwise. An active buzzer is connected to GPIO18 (physical pin 12) and sounds when its control line is driven HIGH. Poll the flame sensor every 500 ms. On a HIGH-to-LOW transition (software edge detection, not continuously while the line stays LOW), log the event with a timestamp to 'alert_log.txt' and activate the buzzer for 2 seconds, then continue. Log a 'System started' entry at startup and a 'System stopped' entry on clean shutdown. Break the 2-second buzzer activation and the 500 ms poll interval into 100 ms slices so the program can respond promptly to shutdown signals. Check every libgpiod call, file operation, and syscall for failure, printing a diagnostic via strerror(errno) to stderr and exiting non-zero if initialization fails. Include the headers errno.h, string.h, time.h, signal.h, unistd.h, stdio.h, stdlib.h, and gpiod.h. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown: turn the buzzer off, release the lines, close the chip, close the log file, and exit cleanly with code 0. Build with: gcc -Wall -Wextra -O2 -o flame_alert flame_alert.c -lgpiod.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to read a SainSmart TTP223B capacitive touch sensor on GPIO4 (physical pin 7) and toggle an LED on GPIO17 (physical pin 11). The TTP223B outputs HIGH (3.3 V) when touched and LOW when released. Configure GPIO4 as input and GPIO17 as output, checking all return values and reporting errors to stderr. Poll GPIO4 every 10 ms; on a rising edge (LOW-to-HIGH transition, not just level), toggle the LED and append a UTC ISO-8601 timestamped line to 'touch_log.txt'. Implement a 200 ms software debounce so a single touch does not register multiple events. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown by turning off the LED, closing the log file, and calling gpioTerminate(). If the log file cannot be opened, print an error and exit non-zero; if a write to it fails, print a warning to stderr but continue running.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library (never wiringPi) to interface with three Texas Instruments TMAG5110A1 Hall-effect latch magnetic sensors on GPIO4, GPIO17, and GPIO27 (BCM numbering). Each sensor's open-drain OUT pin drives a GPIO input with an internal pull-up enabled: it pulls low when a south pole is present and releases high otherwise, so a logic low means magnet-present and a logic high means magnet-removed. Initialize pigpio and verify every GPIO mode and pull call returns 0. Poll all three sensors every 100 ms using gpioDelay, and on the first read record the initial state without falsely logging a transition. Log each state change, with an ISO-8601 timestamp and sensor identifier, to 'magnet_log.txt'. Handle sensor read errors gracefully by logging to stderr and continuing. Install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers for clean shutdown that close the log file and call gpioTerminate(). Include comments explaining the latch behavior.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library (never wiringPi) to read heart-rate data from a Silicon Labs Si1182-A-GM optical heart-rate sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x4A. Initialize pigpio and open the I2C bus, checking every return code. Verify the sensor's PART_ID register (0x00) reads 0x02 and HW_REV register (0x01) reads 0x01, aborting with a clear error if the sensor is absent or wrong. Configure the sensor by writing the LED current (0x3F), averaging (0x04), and enable (0x01) registers, checking each write. Read the 16-bit heart-rate register (0x2A) once per second using i2cReadWordData and convert the raw value to BPM using raw * 0.5. Apply a 5-sample moving average and validate that the filtered BPM is between 30 and 220 before logging. Append valid readings as 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS,BPM' to heart_rate.csv with an immediate flush. Retry on transient I2C read errors without crashing, and implement robust error handling for sensor-absent and bus-error conditions throughout. Handle SIGINT gracefully, closing the I2C handle, terminating pigpio, and closing the log file on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the libgpiod library (never wiringPi) to monitor a Keyes KY-026 flame sensor whose digital-output pin is connected to GPIO17 (Broadcom pin 17, physical pin 11). The sensor's DO pin is active-low: it reads LOW when flame is detected and HIGH when clear. Configure the line as input with an internal pull-up and poll it every 100 ms. When a falling edge is detected (HIGH-to-LOW transition, edge-triggered rather than level-triggered, to avoid duplicate alerts while the signal remains LOW), print 'FLAME DETECTED' to the console and append a line with the current timestamp and 'FLAME DETECTED' to 'flame_log.txt' in append mode, flushing immediately. Check every libgpiod call and file operation, and handle the case where the GPIO chip or line is unavailable. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler for graceful shutdown that releases the GPIO line, closes the chip, and closes the log file on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the libgpiod v2+ bulk/config API (not sysfs, not wiringPi, not the deprecated libgpiod v1 simple API: gpiod_chip_open, gpiod_line_config_new, gpiod_line_settings_new, gpiod_line_settings_set_direction, gpiod_line_config_add_line_settings, gpiod_chip_request_lines, gpiod_line_request_get_value, gpiod_line_request_set_value, gpiod_line_request_release) to read an 8-channel TTP226 capacitive touch sensor module and display an 8-bit binary counter on GPIO outputs. Connect TTP226 outputs OUT1-OUT8, each active-high (3.3 V touched, 0 V idle), to GPIO 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, and 12 respectively (BCM numbering), and drive the counter display on GPIO17 (bit 0, LSB) through GPIO24 (bit 7, MSB). Poll the sensor lines every 10 ms, tracking each line's previous state to detect rising edges (inactive-to-active) without double-counting while held; on each new touch, increment an 8-bit counter that wraps 255 to 0 and immediately update the 8 output GPIOs so bit b appears on GPIO 17+b. Log every touch event to 'touch_log.txt' in append mode as 'YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ, Channel: <1-8>, Counter: <0-255>' and also print 'Touch on channel <N> | Counter: <V>' to stdout. Include a 200 ms stabilization delay after requesting lines before entering the main loop. Check every libgpiod call, file open, and I/O operation, reporting errors with strerror(errno); if gpiod_chip_open fails, print an error and exit non-zero; if any line-request call fails, release everything acquired so far and exit non-zero; if a sensor read errors, log to stderr and skip that channel without crashing; if an output write fails, log to stderr and continue; if the log file cannot be opened, log a warning to stderr and continue with stdout output. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown by resetting all output pins to 0, releasing all libgpiod resources, closing the chip, and exiting cleanly with status 0. Build with: gcc -O2 -Wall -Wextra -o touch_counter touch_counter.c -lgpiod.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the libgpiod library for GPIO control and the Linux i2c-dev ioctl interface (not wiringPi) to interface with a TCS34725 color sensor over I2C bus /dev/i2c-1 (BCM pins 2/3) at its fixed address 0x29. Initialize the sensor by powering it on (PON) and enabling RGBC (AEN), set the integration time to approximately 154 ms (ATIME=0x00) and gain to 1x (CONTROL=0x00), and verify the sensor ID register (0x12) returns 0x44 before proceeding. Read all four 16-bit channel registers as little-endian pairs: clear (0x14), red (0x16), green (0x18), and blue (0x1A). Apply per-channel gain and offset calibration and display the calibrated RGB and clear (C) values on the console. Drive an LED on GPIO17 HIGH when the calibrated red value exceeds a threshold of 200, and LOW otherwise. Check every open, ioctl, read, and write return value; attempt sensor re-initialization on a read failure. Ensure clean resource release, closing the I2C file descriptor, releasing the GPIO line, and powering down the sensor, on all exit paths including SIGINT and SIGTERM. Poll the sensor every 200 ms.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library (never wiringPi) to control the brightness of a 10-LED WS2812B strip connected to GPIO18 (PCM_CLK/GPIO18), generating the precise WS2812B timing waveform via pigpio's hardware PWM/wave functionality. Read ambient light levels from a BH1750 I2C digital light sensor at address 0x23 using continuous high-resolution mode (command 0x10): wait approximately 180 ms after issuing the command, then read 2 bytes and compute lux = (MSB<<8 | LSB) / 1.2. Implement a smooth, non-linear (logarithmic) brightness mapping from the light-sensor readings (0-1000 lux) to LED strip brightness. Gracefully handle I2C errors and sensor-absent conditions with retries, and cleanly release all resources on SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads ambient light from a BH1750 I2C sensor at address 0x23 and adjusts the brightness of an APA102 LED strip via SPI proportionally to the measured lux. Initialize the BH1750 in One-Time High-Resolution mode (command 0x20), wait approximately 120 ms for the conversion to complete, then read the 2-byte result and convert to lux using lux = raw / 1.2. Map the lux range [10, 300] to the APA102's 5-bit global brightness [0, 31]. Send an APA102 frame consisting of a 32-bit zero start frame, one 32-bit LED frame per LED (0xE0 | brightness, blue, green, red), and a 32-bit 0xFF end frame, using a 1 MHz SPI clock. Handle SIGINT gracefully by turning off the LEDs and closing all file descriptors. Implement robust error handling for all I/O operations, sensor-absent scenarios, and bus errors.

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <signal.h>
#include <pigpio.h>

#define LED_PIN 5
#define DELAY 750

void sigint_handler(int sig)
{
    gpioWrite(LED_PIN, 0);
    gpioTerminate();
    exit(0);
}

int main(void)
{
    if (gpioInitialise() < 0)
    {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to initialize pigpio\n");
        return 1;
    }

    gpioSetMode(LED_PIN, PI_OUTPUT);

    signal(SIGINT, sigint_handler);

    while (1)
    {
        gpioWrite(LED_PIN, 1);
        printf("LED ON\n");
        fflush(stdout);
        gpioDelay(DELAY * 1000);

        gpioWrite(LED_PIN, 0);
        printf("LED OFF\n");
        fflush(stdout);
        gpioDelay(DELAY * 1000);
    }

    return 0;
}
```

The program enters an infinite loop, where it turns the LED on, prints 'LED ON', waits 750 ms, turns the LED off, prints 'LED OFF', waits another 750 ms, and flushes stdout after each print so output is visible immediately.

The program handles SIGINT gracefully: cleanly turns off the LED, terminates pigpio, and exits with code 0, ensuring all pigpio resources are released on exit, including on error paths.

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdbool.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <errno.h>
#include <fcntl.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <time.h>
#include <sys/ioctl.h>
#include <linux/i2c-dev.h>

#define I2C_ADDR 0x69
#define I2C_BUS 1
#define I2C_DEV "/dev/i2c-1"
#define I2C_WHO_AM_I 0x0F
#define I2C_WHO_AM_I_EXPECTED 0xD3
#define I2C_CTRL_REG1 0x20
#define I2C_CTRL_REG1_VALUE 0x0F
#define I2C_CTRL_REG4 0x23
#define I2C_CTRL_REG4_VALUE 0x00
#define I2C_OUT_X_L 0x28
#define I2C_OUT_X_H 0x29
#define I2C_OUT_Y_L 0x2A
#define I2C_OUT_Y_H 0x2B
#define I2C_OUT_Z_L 0x2C
#define I2C_OUT_Z_H 0x2D
#define I2C_OUT_X_Y_Z_LEN 6
#define I2C_SENSITIVITY 0.00875
#define I2C_CALIBRATION_SAMPLES 100
#define I2C_CALIBRATION_THRESHOLD 50
#define I2C_LOG_FILE "gyro_log.txt"
#define I2C_LOG_PERIOD_MS 50

static int i2c_fd = -1;
static FILE *log_file = NULL;
static int32_t x_offset = 0;
static int32_t y_offset = 0;
static int32_t z_offset = 0;

static void i2c_init(void)
{
    int ret;

    i2c_fd = open(I2C_DEV, O_RDWR);
    if (i2c_fd < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to open I2C device: %s\n", strerror(errno));
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    ret = ioctl(i2c_fd, I2C_SLAVE, I2C_ADDR);
    if (ret < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to set I2C address: %s\n", strerror(errno));
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    uint8_t buf[1];

    buf[0] = I2C_WHO_AM_I;
    ret = write(i2c_fd, buf, sizeof(buf));
    if (ret < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to write I2C register: %s\n", strerror(errno));
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    ret = read(i2c_fd, buf, sizeof(buf));
    if (ret < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to read I2C register: %s\n", strerror(errno));
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    if (buf[0] != I2C_WHO_AM_I_EXPECTED) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to read I2C WHO_AM_I: 0x%02X\n", buf[0]);
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    buf[0] = I2C_CTRL_REG1;
    ret = write(i2c_fd, buf, sizeof(buf));
    if (ret < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to write I2C register: %s\n", strerror(errno));
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    buf[0] = I2C_CTRL_REG1_VALUE;
    ret = write(i2c_fd, buf, sizeof(buf));
    if (ret < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to write I2C register: %s\n", strerror(errno));
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    buf[0] = I2C_CTRL_REG4;
    ret = write(i2c_fd, buf, sizeof(buf));
    if (ret < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to write I2C register: %s\n", strerror(errno));
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    buf[0] = I2C_CTRL_REG4_VALUE;
    ret = write(i2c_fd, buf, sizeof(buf));
    if (ret < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to write I2C register: %s\n", strerror(errno));
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
}

static void i2c_deinit(void)
{
    if (i2c_fd >= 0) {
        close(i2c_fd);
        i2c_fd = -1;
    }
}

static void log_init(void)
{
    log_file = fopen(I2C_LOG_FILE, "w");
    if (log_file == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to open log file: %s\n", strerror(errno));
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
}

static void log_deinit(void)
{
    if (log_file != NULL) {
        fclose(log_file);
        log_file = NULL;
    }
}

static void log_line(const char *line)
{
    if (log_file != NULL) {
        fprintf(log_file, "%s\n", line);
        fflush(log_file);
    }
}

static void log_timestamp(void)
{
    struct timespec ts;
    char buf[64];

    if (clock_gettime(CLOCK_REALTIME, &ts) < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to get time: %s\n", strerror(errno));
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    if (strftime(buf, sizeof(buf), "%FT%T%z", gmtime(&ts.tv_sec)) == 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to format time: %s\n", strerror(errno));
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    log_line(buf);
}

static void log_calibration(void)
{
    int ret;
    uint8_t buf[I2C_OUT_X_Y_Z_LEN];
    int32_t x_sum = 0;
    int32_t y_sum = 0;
    int32_t z_sum = 0;

    for (int i = 0; i < I2C_CALIBRATION_SAMPLES; i++) {
        buf[0] = I2C_OUT_X_L | (1 << 7);
        ret = write(i2c_fd, buf, sizeof(buf));
        if (ret < 0) {
            fprintf(stderr, "Failed to write I2C register: %s\n", strerror(errno));
            exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
        }

        ret = read(i2c_fd, buf, sizeof(buf));
        if (ret < 0) {
            fprintf(stderr, "Failed to read I2C register: %s\n", strerror(errno));
            exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
        }

        x_sum += (int16_t)((buf[1] << 8) | buf[0]);
        y_sum += (int16_t)((buf[3] << 8) | buf[2]);
        z_sum += (int16_t)((buf[5] << 8) | buf[4]);

        usleep(I2C_LOG_PERIOD_MS * 1000);
    }

    x_offset = x_sum / I2C_CALIBRATION_SAMPLES;
    y_offset = y_sum / I2C_CALIBRATION_SAMPLES;
    z_offset = z_sum / I2C_CALIBRATION_SAMPLES;
}

static void log_readings(void)
{
    int ret;
    uint8_t buf[I2C_OUT_X_Y_Z_LEN];
    int32_t x;
    int32_t y;
    int32_t z;
    char line[64];

    buf[0] = I2C_OUT_X_L | (1 << 7);
    ret = write(i2c_fd, buf, sizeof(buf));
    if (ret < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to write I2C register: %s\n", strerror(errno));
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    ret = read(i2c_fd, buf, sizeof(buf));
    if (ret < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to read I2C register: %s\n", strerror(errno));
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    x = (int16_t)((buf[1] << 8) | buf[0]) - x_offset;
    y = (int16_t)((buf[3] << 8) | buf[2]) - y_offset;
    z = (int16_t)((buf[5] << 8) | buf[4]) - z_offset;

    if (x > I2C_CALIBRATION_THRESHOLD || x < -I2C_CALIBRATION_THRESHOLD) {
        fprintf(stderr, "X axis exceeds threshold: %d\n", x);
        log_line("X axis exceeds threshold");
    }

    if (y > I2C_CALIBRATION_THRESHOLD || y < -I2C_CALIBRATION_THRESHOLD) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Y axis exceeds threshold: %d\n", y);
        log_line("Y axis exceeds threshold");
    }

    if (z > I2C_CALIBRATION_THRESHOLD || z < -I2C_CALIBRATION_THRESHOLD) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Z axis exceeds threshold: %d\n", z);
        log_line("Z axis exceeds threshold");
    }

    snprintf(line, sizeof(line), "%d,%d,%d", x, y, z);
    log_line(line);
}

static void signal_handler(int signum)
{
    exit(EXIT_SUCCESS);
}

int main(void)
{
    i2c_init();
    log_init();
    log_calibration();
    log_timestamp();

    signal(SIGINT, signal_handler);
    signal(SIGTERM, signal_handler);

    while (true) {
        log_readings();
        usleep(I2C_LOG_PERIOD_MS * 1000);
    }

    log_deinit();
    i2c_deinit();

    return EXIT_SUCCESS;
}

The CTRL_REG1 (0x20) register is configured to 0x0F (normal mode, all axes enabled, 100 Hz ODR) and the CTRL_REG4 (0x23) register is configured to 0x00 (250 dps full-scale, continuous update). The 6-byte OUT_X_L..OUT_Z_H block starting at register 0x28 is read using an auto-increment read, and the raw 16-bit signed values are converted to degrees per second using a sensitivity of 0.00875 dps/LSB. The X, Y, and Z zero-rate offsets are computed by performing a 100-sample stationary calibration at startup. The calibrated X, Y, and Z readings are logged with ISO-8601 timestamps to 'gyro_log.txt' at 20 Hz (50 ms period). The code performs error checking on every open, ioctl, read, and write call. If any error occurs, the program exits with an error message. The code also checks the sensor's WHO_AM_I (register 0x0F, expected 0xD3) to ensure that the sensor is present and responding correctly.

Initialize the accelerometer with CTRL_REG1_A (0x20) set to 0x27 (50 Hz, all axes enabled) and the magnetometer with MR_REG_M (0x02) set to 0x00 (continuous-conversion mode). Read 6 bytes from each sensor: accelerometer data from OUT_X_L_A (0x28) with the auto-increment bit, and magnetometer data from OUT_X_H_M (0x03). Log timestamped heading, acceleration (x, y, z in g), and magnetic field (x, y, z in gauss) to 'compass_log.txt', writing a CSV header if the log file is new. Check every I2C call and handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths. Sample every 100 ms. Use SIGINT/SIGTERM for graceful shutdown that closes the I2C handles and terminates pigpio.

Sample every 100 ms, reading the range status register (0x04d) to detect errors such as overrange or signal failure. If the measured distance is less than 100 mm, log 'DOOR_OPEN'; otherwise log 'DOOR_CLOSED'. Log timestamped readings to 'distance_log.txt'. prompt: Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses pigpio to sample data from two STMicroelectronics IMP23ABSU ultrasonic MEMS microphone sensors on I2C bus 1, simulating a bat echolocation analysis system. The two sensors have distinct I2C addresses: sensor 1 at 0x68 and sensor 2 at 0x69, each exposing a 16-bit data register at 0x01 and a control register at 0x00 that must be written with 0x80 to enable continuous measurement. Read 16-bit signed audio samples from both sensors, timestamp them using CLOCK_REALTIME, compute a basic Time Difference of Arrival (TDOA) by subtracting the two samples, and log the data as CSV to 'audio_log.dat' with columns sec, nsec, sensor1, sensor2, tdoa. Use a 10 ms sampling interval. Verify all pigpio initialization and I2C communication calls; handle sensor-absent or bus-failure paths gracefully by skipping the sample and retrying. Ensure clean resource release (I2C handles, log file, pigpio termination) on all exit paths via a SIGINT signal handler.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to interface over SPI with an Analog Devices ADIS16488A IMU on SPI channel 0 (CE0 on GPIO8) at 1 MHz, SPI mode 3 (CPOL=1, CPHA=1), using pigpio SPI flags 0b11000000000 (bit 9 = CPHA, bit 10 = CPOL, bit 8 = aux SPI off) and 16-bit words. The ADIS16488A read protocol sends a 16-bit word whose MSB is 0 followed by the 7-bit register address; the requested register's data is returned on the next 16-bit transfer, so implement a dummy read or stall of at least 40 microseconds between the request and the data-retrieval transfer. Continuously read gyroscope X, Y, Z from registers X_GYRO=0x04, Y_GYRO=0x06, Z_GYRO=0x08 and accelerometer X, Y, Z from X_ACCEL=0x0A, Y_ACCEL=0x0C, Z_ACCEL=0x0E every 100 ms, converting with sensitivities 0.005 deg/sec/LSB for gyroscope and 0.00025 g/LSB for accelerometer, and log each sample with a millisecond-precision timestamp to a CSV file named "imu_data.csv" whose header row is "timestamp,gyro_x,gyro_y,gyro_z,accel_x,accel_y,accel_z". Use 16-bit little-endian reads for the X, Y, and Z result registers at 0x10, 0x11, and 0x12, sampling once per second, and log the data with timestamps to 'magnetic_field_log.csv', writing the CSV header row on startup if the file does not already exist. Check every syscall (open, ioctl, read, write, fopen, etc.) and handle errors gracefully; if an I2C read fails, log an error to stderr and continue the loop. Implement a signal handler for SIGINT/SIGTERM that cleanly closes the I2C file descriptor and the CSV file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that interfaces with a SparkFun ADXL345 I2C accelerometer on /dev/i2c-1 at address 0x53 via the Linux i2c-dev ioctl interface, and uses libgpiod (never wiringPi) to request a falling-edge interrupt on GPIO17 (physical pin 11), connected to the ADXL345 INT1 pin, to detect freefall events. Put the sensor in standby before register writes, then configure it: set THRESH_FF (0x0A) to ~300 mg, TIME_FF (0x20) to ~100 ms, enable the freefall interrupt via bit 2 of INT_ENABLE (0x2E), map it to INT1 via INT_MAP (0x2F = 0x00), and enter measurement mode by setting POWER_CTL (0x2D) to 0x08. On each interrupt, read INT_SOURCE (0x30) to verify the freefall bit (bit 2) is set, then read 6 bytes from DATAX0 (0x32) in a single I2C block read; reading INT_SOURCE also clears the interrupt. Log timestamped X, Y, Z acceleration values only during a freefall event to 'freefall_log.csv' in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS.mmm,X,Y,Z' (with milliseconds), writing a header row on creation and flushing after each write. Check every I2C syscall and GPIO call, verify the device ID (register 0x00 should read 0xE5) at startup, and handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths. Use a poll-based loop on the libgpiod event file descriptor rather than threads, and on SIGINT/SIGTERM disable the sensor's interrupts, close the I2C file descriptor, release the GPIO lines, close the chip, and close the log file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the libgpiod library (not the deprecated sysfs interface, and not wiringPi) to read an E18-D80NK IR obstacle sensor connected to GPIO17. The E18-D80NK outputs LOW (0) when an obstacle is detected within its detection range, adjustable up to about 80 cm and configured here for roughly 30 cm, and HIGH (1) when the path is clear. Open the gpiochip device for GPIO17 on the Raspberry Pi 5 (gpiochip4) and request the line for input direction using modern libgpiod APIs such as gpiod_chip_open_by_name, gpiod_line_open, gpiod_line_request_input, and gpiod_line_get_value. Poll the sensor every 1 second; when an obstacle is detected (line reads LOW), trigger a simulated "self-parking" sequence logged to the console with timestamps ("Self-parking sequence started" / "completed"). Check all libgpiod calls, handle the case where the gpiochip or line is unavailable and exit gracefully, and handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) for clean shutdown, releasing the GPIO line and closing the chip on all exit paths.

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <time.h>
#include <signal.h>
#include <gpiod.h>

#define GPIO_CHIP_NAME "gpiochip4"
#define GPIO_LINE_NUM 17
#define GPIO_LINE_NAME "gpio17"
#define GPIO_LINE_DIRECTION GPIOD_LINE_DIRECTION_INPUT
#define GPIO_LINE_REQUEST_TYPE GPIOD_LINE_REQUEST_DIRECTION_AS_IS
#define GPIO_LINE_REQUEST_CONSUMER "self-parking"
#define GPIO_LINE_REQUEST_EVENT_TYPE GPIOD_LINE_REQUEST_EVENT_BOTH_EDGES
#define GPIO_LINE_REQUEST_FLAG GPIOD_LINE_REQUEST_FLAG_DEFAULT
#define POLL_INTERVAL_MS 1000

static struct gpiod_chip *chip;
static struct gpiod_line *line;
static int running = 1;

static void sigint_handler(int signum)
{
    running = 0;
}

int main(void)
{
    int ret;
    struct timespec ts;

    // Open the gpiochip device
    chip = gpiod_chip_open_by_name(GPIO_CHIP_NAME);
    if (!chip) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to open gpiochip device %s\n", GPIO_CHIP_NAME);
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    // Request the line for input direction
    line = gpiod_chip_get_line(chip, GPIO_LINE_NUM);
    if (!line) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to get line %d\n", GPIO_LINE_NUM);
        gpiod_chip_close(chip);
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    ret = gpiod_line_request_input(line, GPIO_LINE_REQUEST_CONSUMER);
    if (ret < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to request line %d for input direction\n", GPIO_LINE_NUM);
        gpiod_line_release(line);
        gpiod_chip_close(chip);
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    // Set up signal handler for SIGINT (Ctrl+C)
    signal(SIGINT, sigint_handler);

    // Poll the sensor every 1 second
    while (running) {
        // Read the line value
        int value = gpiod_line_get_value(line);
        if (value < 0) {
            fprintf(stderr, "Failed to read line %d\n", GPIO_LINE_NUM);
            break;
        }

        // Check if an obstacle is detected (line reads LOW)
        if (value == 0) {
            // Trigger a simulated "self-parking" sequence
            printf("Self-parking sequence started\n");
            sleep(5);
            printf("Self-parking sequence completed\n");
        }

        // Wait 1 second
        ts.tv_sec = 0;
        ts.tv_nsec = POLL_INTERVAL_MS * 1000000;
        nanosleep(&ts, NULL);
    }

    // Release the GPIO line and close the chip
    gpiod_line_release(line);
    gpiod_chip_close(chip);

    return EXIT_SUCCESS;
}

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses libgpiod (v2 API) to interface with two Keyes KY-032 IR obstacle avoidance sensors connected to GPIO17 and GPIO27 (physical pins 11 and 13, BCM numbering). The KY-032 output is active-low: the sensor reads 0 when an obstacle is detected and 1 when the path is clear. Use a single gpiochip and request both lines together for input, reading both lines in a single call via the libgpiod v2 bulk-read API gpiod_line_request_get_values. Poll both sensors every 100 ms and log the obstacle detection status to the console with a timestamp, simulating a basic collision avoidance system for a small robot, running in an infinite loop until interrupted. Check every libgpiod call, handle the case where the gpiochip or lines are unavailable, and ensure clean release of all resources on all exit paths including SIGINT (Ctrl+C). Compile cleanly with -Wall -Wextra against libgpiod >= 2.0.

{

    sigaction(SIGINT, &sa, NULL);

    /* Open gpiochip */
    chip = gpiod_chip_open_by_name(GPIOCHIP_NAME);
    if (!chip) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to open gpiochip: %s\n", strerror(errno));
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    }

        goto err_close_line1;
    }

    }

    if (ret < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to commit line request: %s\n", strerror(errno));
        goto err_free_req;
    }

    bulk = gpiod_line_bulk_new(chip);
    if (!bulk) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to create bulk: %s\n", strerror(errno));
        goto err_free_req;
    }
    ret = gpiod_line_bulk_add_line(bulk, line1);
    if (ret < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to add line to bulk: %s\n", strerror(errno));
        goto err_free_bulk;

Initialize the SPI device (/dev/spidev0.0) and a libgpiod line for the CS pin, write to the MSC_CTRL register (0x24) to enable data ready mode, then periodically read the X, Y, and Z angular rate output registers (0x04, 0x06, 0x08) using the ADIS16266 two-transfer read protocol (send the address with the MSB set, then read 2 bytes). Convert the raw 16-bit signed values to angular rates using the scale factor of 0.02 deg/sec/LSB and log the results to the console every 100 ms. Include robust error handling: check all SPI and GPIO initialization calls, handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including SIGINT, running in a loop until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses only the pigpio C API, not wiringPi, to read accelerometer and gyroscope data from an STMicroelectronics LSM6DSR connected via I2C bus 1 at the 7-bit address 0x6B. Initialize the pigpio library and open the I2C bus, then verify the sensor is present by reading the WHO_AM_I register and checking it returns 0x6B. Configure the accelerometer for +-2g full-scale at 104 Hz (CTRL1_XL = 0x42) and the gyroscope for +-250 dps at 104 Hz (CTRL2_G = 0x42). Every 100 ms, burst-read 12 bytes starting at OUTX_L_G (0x22) covering gyro X/Y/Z then accel X/Y/Z, convert to physical units using gyro sensitivity mdps/LSB = 8.75 (i.e. 0.00875 dps/LSB) and accel sensitivity mg/LSB = 0.061 (i.e. 0.000061 g/LSB), and print one line to stdout. Handle all error paths: pigpio init failure, I2C open failure, WHO_AM_I mismatch, register write failures, and short or failed burst reads, printing to stderr and exiting non-zero; check every I2C call's return value and never use hard-coded sleeps that ignore errors. Install a SIGINT handler so Ctrl+C triggers a clean shutdown that closes the I2C handle and calls gpioTerminate() before exiting.

Read X, Y, Z data from registers 0x32-0x37, calculate tilt angles using atan2, and log events with timestamps every 100 ms. Log tilt events exceeding a threshold of 30.0 degrees to '/var/log/tilt_events.log'. Include robust error handling for I2C communication failures, explicitly handling sensor-absent and bus-error paths, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including signal handling for Ctrl+C.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library, and no wiringPi, to monitor ambient noise levels via a KY-038 sound sensor connected to GPIO17 (physical pin 11). The KY-038 OUT pin is active-high and pulses when sound exceeds its onboard comparator threshold. Accept a single command-line argument — an integer threshold representing the minimum number of high-readings per 5-second window required to trigger an alert — and validate it, rejecting non-numeric or non-positive values. Continuously sample GPIO17 every 1 ms for 5 seconds, counting how many times the pin reads high; at the end of each 5-second window, print a timestamped ALERT to stdout if the high-reading count exceeds the threshold, otherwise print a normal status line. Run in a continuous loop until signaled to stop, with a 1-second pause between monitoring windows. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM gracefully, terminating pigpio and exiting cleanly, and check every pigpio call for failure (gpioInitialise, gpioSetMode), printing clear error messages to stderr on any failure.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the libgpiod C API, never wiringPi, to control two 12V electromagnetic door locks actuated by 5V active-HIGH relay modules driven via TIP120 transistors on GPIO17 (Door A) and GPIO27 (Door B), based on a randomly generated 6-digit security code. Initialize GPIO17 and GPIO27 as outputs, both defaulting to LOW (locks energized/closed); a HIGH signal de-energizes the relay and unlocks the corresponding door. Generate a random 6-digit code between 100000 and 999999 at startup and print it to stdout. In a loop, prompt the user to enter the code via stdin; if it matches, unlock Door A (GPIO17 HIGH) for 5 seconds, then re-lock it (LOW), log the successful entry to 'access_log.txt' as a CSV row 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS,NNNNNN', and generate a new random code. If the code does not match, print 'Access denied' and continue; handle invalid non-numeric stdin input gracefully by clearing the buffer and re-prompting. Check every libgpiod call (chip open, line get, line request) and file open, printing meaningful errors to stderr and exiting non-zero on initialization failure. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that sets a volatile sig_atomic_t flag so the main loop exits cleanly; on exit, drive both GPIO outputs LOW (locked), release all libgpiod resources (lines and chip), and close any open file handles. Compile with: gcc -Wall -o door_access door_access.c -lgpiod.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses pigpio for I2C and hardware PWM to implement a theremin using an MPR121 capacitive touch sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x5A. The program acts as a TCP server listening on port 12345; when a client sends a message starting with 'MOTION_DETECTED:' and containing the shared secret 'MySecretKey', the theremin plays tones for 5 seconds based on capacitive touch readings, using hardware PWM on GPIO18. Initialize the MPR121 with proper soft-reset and electrode configuration, and map the maximum electrode filtered data value to a frequency in the range 220-880 Hz using a logarithmic scale, sampling touch values every 20 ms during the 5-second playback window and logging each frequency to 'frequency_log.txt'. Handle errors for pigpio initialization, I2C open/read, and socket/bind/listen/accept. On SIGINT/SIGTERM, stop PWM, close I2C and sockets, and terminate pigpio cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that interfaces with an LSM303DLHC magnetometer via I2C bus 1 at default address 0x1E, connected to the physical SDA1/SCL1 pins, and controls an LED on GPIO17. Use libgpiod for GPIO/PWM control and the standard Linux I2C interface (/dev/i2c-1, ioctl) for sensor communication, not wiringPi. Initialize the magnetometer by writing 0x18 to CTRL_REG1_M (0x20) for 10 Hz continuous conversion, and read 6 bytes of data starting from OUT_X_L_M (0x08) in a single I2C block read. The program must read X, Y, Z magnetic field data, compute the magnitude of the Z-axis field, and adjust the LED brightness proportionally using hardware PWM, sampling every 100 ms in the main loop. Handle I2C errors (e.g., sensor absent, bus errors) gracefully by logging the error and skipping the sample without crashing, and implement clean resource release on SIGINT/SIGTERM by releasing the PWM, closing the I2C file descriptor, and closing any log files.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to interface with an HMC5883L magnetometer via I2C on bus 1 at address 0x1E. Configure the sensor for 8-sample averaging, 15 Hz output rate, and a gain setting of 1.3 Gauss (Configuration Register A = 0x70, Configuration Register B = 0x20, Mode register = 0x00 for continuous mode). Continuously collect raw readings to compute hard-iron offsets as a running average over a 100-sample window. Every 500 ms, apply the current hard-iron offsets to the latest raw reading and print the offset-corrected (not unit-normalized) X, Y, and Z values to stdout. Explicitly flag any I2C read/write errors on stderr without crashing, and ensure clean resource release of the I2C handle and pigpio library on SIGINT/SIGTERM. Do not use FIFOs or secondary processes.
