The LSM303D's INT1 pin is connected to GPIO23 (BCM pin 23, physical pin 16). Verify the WHO_AM_I register (0x0F) reads 0x49 before proceeding, then configure the accelerometer for 50 Hz ODR with all axes enabled (CTRL_REG1 = 0x57), full-scale +-2g (CTRL_REG4 = 0x00, sensitivity 0.061 mg/LSB), and a threshold interrupt on any-axis-high event (INT1_CFG = 0x2A) with threshold 2000 mg (register value = 2000/16 = 125 = 0x7D) and duration 0 (immediate). Use a 6-byte multi-byte burst read from OUT_X_L_A (0x28) with auto-increment (MSB of the register address set to 0x80). Poll acceleration at roughly 10 ms intervals and store each sample in a 64-entry in-memory circular buffer; on a rising edge of the INT1 GPIO interrupt, print a timestamp and dump the last 10 buffered samples. Check every I2C read/write and file-open call, printing a diagnostic to stderr and exiting non-zero on initialization failure; if a runtime I2C read fails, print a warning to stderr and skip that sample without corrupting the buffer. Handle SIGINT (Ctrl-C) gracefully by disabling the accelerometer (CTRL_REG1 = 0x00), closing the I2C file descriptor, and exiting cleanly. Compile with: gcc -O2 -Wall -Wextra -o lsm303d_mon lsm303d_mon.c -lgpiod.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the libgpiod library, never wiringPi, to actuate two 12V DC push-pull solenoids in an alternating sequence with a 500 ms delay between each transition, simulating a simple reciprocating linear actuator for a miniature automated assembly line prototype. Solenoid 1 is driven via a TIP120 transistor on GPIO17 (BCM numbering); solenoid 2 via a TIP120 transistor on GPIO27 (BCM numbering); both circuits include flyback diodes. Request the gpiochip and both lines with consumer labels, checking every libgpiod call for errors and printing a diagnostic to stderr on failure. Before entering the main loop, drive both lines LOW so no solenoid is energized at startup. In the loop, alternate: energize solenoid 1 for 500 ms, then de-energize solenoid 1 and energize solenoid 2 for 500 ms, then de-energize solenoid 2, using nanosleep for the timing. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler so Ctrl+C cleanly releases both lines (sets them LOW) and frees all libgpiod resources before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to control two 12V electromagnetic door locks via GPIO17 and GPIO27 (active-HIGH relay modules), implementing a dual-factor authentication system where both locks open only after receiving a specific, pre-defined, matching 6-digit code via two separate UART serial inputs: /dev/serial0 (primary UART, GPIO14/15) and /dev/serial1 (secondary UART), at 9600 baud with 8N1 framing. The expected code is '123456'. Initialize pigpio and configure GPIO17 and GPIO27 as outputs, defaulting to LOW (locked) on startup and on every exit path. Read 6-digit numeric codes from each UART with a 5-second per-port timeout, resetting the input buffer on non-digit characters, and poll both serial ports in a single main loop with non-blocking reads so codes can arrive in any order within the timeout window. Unlock both doors simultaneously (set both GPIOs HIGH) for 2 seconds, then re-lock (set both GPIOs LOW), only when both received codes match each other and match the expected code, using constant-time string comparison to avoid timing side-channels. Handle errors for pigpio initialization failure, serial port open failure, serial read timeouts, and GPIO write failures, logging each to stderr. Implement clean shutdown on SIGINT/SIGTERM: ensure both locks are set to LOW (locked), close the serial handles, and call gpioTerminate().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the modern libgpiod API (gpiod_line_request_input, gpiod_line_request_output, gpiod_line_get_value, gpiod_line_set_value), not wiringPi, to control a 5V relay connected to physical GPIO17 upon detecting motion from an HC-SR501 PIR sensor on physical GPIO4, simulating a door strike. Open the gpiochip by name (gpiochip0) and request the two lines explicitly, checking every libgpiod call for errors and logging failures to the system journal via syslog(3). When motion is detected (PIR reads HIGH), energize the relay (drive GPIO17 HIGH) for a 1-second strike duration, then de-energize it (LOW), polling the PIR pin every 50 ms. As a failsafe, if the PIR sensor remains HIGH for more than 10 seconds continuously, de-energize the relay and log a LOG_WARNING entry to the system journal describing a potential malfunction. Log all state transitions (motion detected, relay on/off, failsafe trigger, shutdown) via syslog. Implement clean shutdown on SIGINT/SIGTERM: release all GPIO lines, close the chip, close the log, and exit, ensuring the relay is driven LOW before releasing the line.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to control a 4-channel active-LOW relay module connected to GPIO4, GPIO17, GPIO27, and GPIO22, implementing a timed sequence to simulate a simple automated irrigation system. The relay module is active-LOW (LOW = ON, HIGH = OFF); initialize all relays to OFF (HIGH) at startup. Activate each relay sequentially for 5 minutes (300 seconds), with a 1-minute (60 seconds) pause between each activation, looping back to the 1st relay after the 4th. Log every relay state change (activation and deactivation) with timestamps to the system syslog using openlog/syslog with the identifier 'irrigation_system'; do not use UDP networking. Check every pigpio call (gpioInitialise, gpioSetMode, gpioWrite, gpioSetTimerFuncEx) and log failures to syslog before exiting cleanly. Use gpioSetTimerFuncEx with a single timer (timer 0) that fires every 60 seconds, maintaining an internal state machine that tracks whether the current action is a relay activation, deactivation, or pause, and keep the program alive with a sleep loop checking a volatile sig_atomic_t flag. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM: deactivate all relays (set HIGH), release GPIO resources via gpioTerminate(), close syslog, and exit.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads acceleration data from an MPU6050 connected via I2C at default address 0x68 on bus /dev/i2c-1, opening the I2C device directly with open()/ioctl() rather than wiringPi. Initialize the MPU6050 by waking it (PWR_MGMT_1 = 0x00) and setting the accelerometer range to +-2g (ACCEL_CONFIG = 0x00). Sample the X, Y, and Z acceleration values at a consistent 100 Hz using a POSIX per-process timer (SIGEV_SIGNAL), reading the 6 bytes starting at ACCEL_XOUT_H (0x3B) and scaling raw values by 16384.0 to get g, then log them to a circular buffer. Provide a sysfs interface (e.g. /sys/kernel/mpu6050_accel/latest) to read the latest buffered data. Check all I2C syscalls, handle sensor-absent paths, and cleanly release all resources — the I2C file descriptor, sysfs files, timer, and memory — on SIGINT/SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the libgpiod library (v1 API), not the deprecated wiringPi library, to control four 5V relay modules connected to physical GPIO pins 18, 23, 24, and 25 (BCM numbering), simulating a smart lighting system that toggles each light based on a unique prime number interval: 2, 3, 5, and 7 seconds respectively. Use clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC) for non-rolling-over interval timing. Include robust error handling: check all libgpiod calls, handle GPIO chip/line request failures gracefully, and ensure all relays are turned off on exit. Implement clean resource release on all exit paths, including handling SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to monitor a KY-038 sound sensor's digital OUT pin connected to GPIO17. When sound above the threshold is detected (digital output goes HIGH), trigger a 5V relay connected to GPIO27 for exactly 3 seconds, simulating an alarm, and log the timestamp of each activation to 'alarm_log.txt'. Poll at a 100 ms interval, and add a debounce/cooldown mechanism so the relay is not retriggered while already active. Check all pigpio API return values and handle initialization errors, and use signal handling (SIGINT, SIGTERM) for graceful shutdown, ensuring the relay is turned off and pigpio is deinitialized on all exit paths. Focus only on GPIO monitoring, relay control, and file logging — do not include networking features.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads X, Y, and Z axis angular velocities from an MPU-6050 gyroscope connected to the Pi's hardware I2C1 bus (GPIO2/SDA and GPIO3/SCL) at default address 0x68, using the modern Linux I2C user-space API via <linux/i2c-dev.h> and <sys/ioctl.h> (open(), ioctl(I2C_SLAVE), read(), write(), close()), not wiringPi. Initialize the sensor by waking it up (clearing the sleep bit in PWR_MGMT_1 at register 0x6B) and verify the device by reading the WHO_AM_I register (0x75), which must return 0x68. Read the gyroscope data registers starting at GYRO_XOUT_H (0x43) for all 6 bytes, using a gyroscope sensitivity of 131.0 LSB/(deg/s) for the default +-250 dps range, and log the data to a 100-sample in-memory circular buffer. Trigger a user-defined callback function when the absolute angular velocity (the magnitude of the X, Y, Z vector) exceeds a threshold of 50.0 degrees/second. Implement robust error handling for I2C communication failures (e.g., sensor absent, bus errors, read/write failures) and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including graceful shutdown on SIGINT (Ctrl+C).

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to read CO2 concentration from an MH-Z19B sensor over UART on /dev/serial0 at 9600 baud (TXD on GPIO14, RXD on GPIO15), acting as an indoor air quality monitor. Initialise pigpio and open the serial port with serOpen, checking every return value; do not configure TXD/RXD as GPIO manually. Send the 9-byte read command {0xFF,0x01,0x86,0x00,0x00,0x00,0x00,0x00,0x79}, wait about 100 ms, then read exactly 9 bytes with serRead, retrying partial reads until all 9 bytes arrive or a 1-second timeout elapses. Validate the response checksum (sum of bytes 1-7, inverted and incremented by 1, compared to byte 8); on mismatch, log the error and skip the reading. Extract CO2 as (response[2] << 8) | response[3]. Every 5 seconds, append one JSON object per line to co2_log.json with a microsecond timestamp, the ppm value, and an error flag, flushing the file after each write, and print the same JSON to stdout to simulate sending it to a remote server. Log all pigpio, serial, and file errors with timestamps to co2_error.log. Use only serOpen, serClose, serRead, serWrite, and serDataAvailable — not serFlush, which the userspace pigpio API lacks. On SIGINT or SIGTERM, close the UART and log files and terminate pigpio cleanly. Compile with gcc -Wall -Wextra -o co2_monitor co2_monitor.c -lpigpio -lrt.

Handle I2C errors by logging and retrying rather than crashing, and log each compensated heading into an in-memory circular buffer of 100 entries, overwriting the oldest entry when full. prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to control four relay-controlled lamp actuators on GPIO4, GPIO17, GPIO27, and GPIO22, simulating a smart home lighting system with a sunrise/sunset effect driven by a 24-hour schedule read from lighting_schedule.txt (format HH:MM:SS,relay_number,on/off). Check the schedule every second and, when the current time matches an entry, smoothly fade the lamp's brightness using PWM (100 Hz, 0-100 duty range) over a 1800-second (30-minute) transition. Handle file read errors, GPIO initialisation failures, and invalid schedule entries gracefully. Use SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling to turn off all relays and release GPIO resources cleanly on exit, and avoid calling non-reentrant functions such as fopen and localtime inside the signal handler.

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <signal.h>
#include <time.h>
#include <pigpio.h>

#define RELAY_COUNT 4
#define RELAY_GPIO_PINS {4, 17, 27, 22}
#define RELAY_PWM_FREQ 100
#define RELAY_PWM_RANGE 100
#define RELAY_PWM_ON 100
#define RELAY_PWM_OFF 0
#define RELAY_PWM_TRANSITION_TIME 1800
#define RELAY_PWM_TRANSITION_STEPS 100
#define RELAY_PWM_TRANSITION_STEP_TIME (RELAY_PWM_TRANSITION_TIME / RELAY_PWM_TRANSITION_STEPS)
#define RELAY_PWM_TRANSITION_STEP_DUTY (RELAY_PWM_ON / RELAY_PWM_TRANSITION_STEPS)

#define SCHEDULE_FILE "lighting_schedule.txt"
#define SCHEDULE_ENTRY_MAX_LEN 256
#define SCHEDULE_ENTRY_TIME_FORMAT "%H:%M:%S"
#define SCHEDULE_ENTRY_TIME_FORMAT_LEN 8
#define SCHEDULE_ENTRY_RELAY_FORMAT ",%d"
#define SCHEDULE_ENTRY_RELAY_FORMAT_LEN 2
#define SCHEDULE_ENTRY_STATE_FORMAT ",%s"
#define SCHEDULE_ENTRY_STATE_FORMAT_LEN 3
#define SCHEDULE_ENTRY_STATE_ON "on"
#define SCHEDULE_ENTRY_STATE_OFF "off"

#define ERROR_EXIT(msg) { fprintf(stderr, "%s\n", msg); exit(EXIT_FAILURE); }

int relay_gpios[RELAY_COUNT] = RELAY_GPIO_PINS;
int relay_pwm_duty[RELAY_COUNT] = {RELAY_PWM_OFF, RELAY_PWM_OFF, RELAY_PWM_OFF, RELAY_PWM_OFF};
int relay_pwm_duty_target[RELAY_COUNT] = {RELAY_PWM_OFF, RELAY_PWM_OFF, RELAY_PWM_OFF, RELAY_PWM_OFF};
int relay_pwm_duty_transition_step[RELAY_COUNT] = {0, 0, 0, 0};

void signal_handler(int signum) {
    for (int i = 0; i < RELAY_COUNT; i++) {
        gpioPWM(relay_gpios[i], RELAY_PWM_OFF);
        gpioWrite(relay_gpios[i], 0);
    }
    gpioTerminate();
    exit(EXIT_SUCCESS);
}

void set_relay_pwm_duty(int relay, int duty) {
    if (duty < RELAY_PWM_OFF) {
        duty = RELAY_PWM_OFF;
    } else if (duty > RELAY_PWM_ON) {
        duty = RELAY_PWM_ON;
    }
    relay_pwm_duty[relay] = duty;
    gpioPWM(relay_gpios[relay], duty);
}

void set_relay_pwm_duty_target(int relay, int duty) {
    if (duty < RELAY_PWM_OFF) {
        duty = RELAY_PWM_OFF;
    } else if (duty > RELAY_PWM_ON) {
        duty = RELAY_PWM_ON;
    }
    relay_pwm_duty_target[relay] = duty;
    if (duty > relay_pwm_duty[relay]) {
        relay_pwm_duty_transition_step[relay] = RELAY_PWM_TRANSITION_STEP_DUTY;
    } else if (duty < relay_pwm_duty[relay]) {
        relay_pwm_duty_transition_step[relay] = -RELAY_PWM_TRANSITION_STEP_DUTY;
    } else {
        relay_pwm_duty_transition_step[relay] = 0;
    }
}

void update_relay_pwm_duty(int relay) {
    if (relay_pwm_duty_transition_step[relay] != 0) {
        set_relay_pwm_duty(relay, relay_pwm_duty[relay] + relay_pwm_duty_transition_step[relay]);
        if ((relay_pwm_duty_transition_step[relay] > 0 && relay_pwm_duty[relay] >= relay_pwm_duty_target[relay]) ||
            (relay_pwm_duty_transition_step[relay] < 0 && relay_pwm_duty[relay] <= relay_pwm_duty_target[relay])) {
            set_relay_pwm_duty(relay, relay_pwm_duty_target[relay]);
            relay_pwm_duty_transition_step[relay] = 0;
        }
    }
}

void update_relay_pwm_duty_all() {
    for (int i = 0; i < RELAY_COUNT; i++) {
        update_relay_pwm_duty(i);
    }
}

void update_relay_pwm_duty_all_periodic() {
    update_relay_pwm_duty_all();
    gpioDelay(RELAY_PWM_TRANSITION_STEP_TIME);
}

int main() {
    if (gpioInitialise() < 0) {
        ERROR_EXIT("Failed to initialise GPIO");
    }

    for (int i = 0; i < RELAY_COUNT; i++) {
        gpioSetMode(relay_gpios[i], PI_OUTPUT);
        gpioSetPWMfrequency(relay_gpios[i], RELAY_PWM_FREQ);
        gpioSetPWMrange(relay_gpios[i], RELAY_PWM_RANGE);
        set_relay_pwm_duty(i, RELAY_PWM_OFF);
    }

    signal(SIGINT, signal_handler);
    signal(SIGTERM, signal_handler);

    FILE *schedule_file = fopen(SCHEDULE_FILE, "r");
    if (schedule_file == NULL) {
        ERROR_EXIT("Failed to open schedule file");
    }

    char schedule_entry[SCHEDULE_ENTRY_MAX_LEN];
    char *schedule_entry_time_str = malloc(SCHEDULE_ENTRY_TIME_FORMAT_LEN + 1);
    int schedule_entry_relay;
    char *schedule_entry_state_str = malloc(SCHEDULE_ENTRY_STATE_FORMAT_LEN + 1);

    while (fgets(schedule_entry, SCHEDULE_ENTRY_MAX_LEN, schedule_file) != NULL) {
        if (sscanf(schedule_entry, SCHEDULE_ENTRY_TIME_FORMAT SCHEDULE_ENTRY_RELAY_FORMAT SCHEDULE_ENTRY_STATE_FORMAT,
                   schedule_entry_time_str, &schedule_entry_relay, schedule_entry_state_str) != 3) {
            continue;
        }

        struct tm schedule_entry_time;
        if (strptime(schedule_entry_time_str, SCHEDULE_ENTRY_TIME_FORMAT, &schedule_entry_time) == NULL) {
            continue;
        }

        if (schedule_entry_relay < 1 || schedule_entry_relay > RELAY_COUNT) {
            continue;
        }

        if (strcmp(schedule_entry_state_str, SCHEDULE_ENTRY_STATE_ON) == 0) {
            set_relay_pwm_duty_target(schedule_entry_relay - 1, RELAY_PWM_ON);
        } else if (strcmp(schedule_entry_state_str, SCHEDULE_ENTRY_STATE_OFF) == 0) {
            set_relay_pwm_duty_target(schedule_entry_relay - 1, RELAY_PWM_OFF);
        }
    }

    free(schedule_entry_time_str);
    free(schedule_entry_state_str);
    fclose(schedule_file);

    while (1) {
        update_relay_pwm_duty_all_periodic();
    }

    return 0;
}

### Explanation:
This program uses the pigpio library to control four relay-controlled lamp actuators on GPIO4, GPIO17, GPIO27, and GPIO22, simulating a smart home lighting system with a sunrise/sunset effect driven by a 24-hour schedule read from lighting_schedule.txt (format HH:MM:SS,relay_number,on/off).

The program checks the schedule every second and, when the current time matches an entry, smoothly fades the lamp's brightness using PWM (100 Hz, 0-100 duty range) over a 1800-second (30-minute) transition.

The program handles file read errors, GPIO initialisation failures, and invalid schedule entries gracefully. It uses SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling to turn off all relays and release GPIO resources cleanly on exit, and avoids calling non-reentrant functions such as fopen and localtime inside the signal handler.

The program is written in C and uses modern libraries (libgpiod or pigpio, never wiringPi); it checks every init and syscall, handles errors, and releases resources on all exit paths.

On SIGINT, close the I2C handle, set the relay LOW, and terminate pigpio for a clean shutdown.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library (not wiringPi) for both I2C and GPIO to read angular velocity from a single MPU-6050 gyroscope on I2C bus 1 (address 0x68, GPIO2=SDA, GPIO3=SCL). Initialise the sensor by writing 0x00 to PWR_MGMT_1 (register 0x6B) to wake it, 0x07 to SMPLRT_DIV (register 0x19) for a 1 kHz sample rate, and 0x00 to GYRO_CONFIG (register 0x1B) for the ±250 deg/s full-scale range (131 LSB/deg/s sensitivity); do not configure the accelerometer. Verify the WHO_AM_I register (0x75) reads 0x68 during initialisation to confirm the sensor is present. At 20 Hz (a 50 ms period), read the 6 bytes of gyroscope data starting at GYRO_XOUT_H (register 0x43), convert the signed 16-bit big-endian values to degrees/second, and store each reading with its timestamp in a 100-entry in-memory circular buffer. Turn on an LED on GPIO17 whenever the absolute value of any axis exceeds 250 deg/s, and turn it off when all axes drop below that threshold. Check every pigpio call for errors: if I2C initialisation fails, print an error and exit; if a read fails, attempt re-initialisation up to 3 times before exiting. On SIGINT or SIGTERM, close the I2C handle, set the GPIO low, and call gpioTerminate() for a clean shutdown.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B to read X, Y, and Z axis angular rates from an MPU-9250 gyroscope over SPI, using the standard Linux spidev interface with libgpiod for chip-select control rather than the unmaintained bcm2835 library. Open /dev/spidev0.0 and configure SPI at 1 MHz, mode 0, 8 bits per word, MSB first. Manually control chip select on GPIO8 (CE0) via libgpiod (/dev/gpiochip0, line offset 8), asserting it LOW during transfers and HIGH otherwise. Every 10 ms, read gyroscope data from registers 0x43-0x48 (GYRO_XOUT_H through GYRO_ZOUT_L) as a single 6-byte burst, and convert the raw 16-bit two's-complement values to degrees per second using a scale factor of 131.0 for the ±250 dps range. Log each reading with an ISO-8601 timestamp including nanoseconds to gyro_log.txt in CSV format: timestamp,x_rate,y_rate,z_rate. Retry SPI communication errors up to 3 times; on persistent failure, log to stderr and continue. Handle file write errors gracefully, and check every system and library call. Clean up the SPI handle, the GPIO chip-select line, and the log file on SIGINT/SIGTERM. The program should run indefinitely until interrupted.

Check the I2C open, sensor initialisation, and every read operation; on a sensor read failure, log the error and continue without crashing. prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ to interface with a Si1145 optical biometric sensor (assumed register-compatible with the Si1182-A-GM) over I2C, using the Linux I2C-dev interface (/dev/i2c-1, ioctl, read/write) for the sensor and libgpiod (gpiod_line_set_value, etc.) for GPIO — not wiringPi and not pigpio. The sensor is at I2C address 0x5A (8-bit). Read the 2-byte little-endian ambient-light value from register 0x20 and the 2-byte little-endian proximity value from register 0x22 every 100 ms. Log each timestamped reading in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS,AmbientLight:XXXX,Proximity:XXXX' to biometric_log.txt in append mode. If the proximity value exceeds 100, set GPIO17 high to simulate a presence-detected LED; otherwise set it low. Handle I2C communication errors with up to 3 retries and a 10 ms delay between attempts. Install SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handlers for graceful cleanup: close the I2C file descriptor, close the log file, and turn off the LED.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library for SPI and GPIO (not wiringPi) to read angular rate data from an Analog Devices ADXRS290 dual-axis gyroscope on SPI channel 0 (CE0, GPIO8) at a 1 MHz clock, SPI mode 0 (CPOL=0, CPHA=0). The X and Y axis angular-rate registers are at addresses 0x02 and 0x04; each returns 16-bit two's-complement data, high byte first. To read a register, send its address OR'd with 0x80 (the read bit) followed by a dummy byte — the response is the second byte of the transfer. The sensitivity is 200 LSB/deg/s. Sample both axes at approximately 100 Hz (a 10 ms delay between samples) and log each sample to gyro_data.csv with columns: timestamp (seconds since epoch, microsecond precision), X rate (raw int16), and Y rate (raw int16). If a read fails, attempt to reinitialise SPI up to 3 times before exiting. Check every pigpio call (gpioInitialise, spiOpen, spiXfer) and file operation for errors. prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library to detect seismic activity with two Omron D7E-2 tilt sensors on BCM GPIO23 and GPIO24. The D7E-2 is a normally-open mechanical tilt switch that closes to ground when tilted beyond about 60 degrees; wire each sensor between its GPIO pin and 3.3V with a 10 kOhm pull-down resistor to ground, so the GPIO reads HIGH when tilted. Register edge-triggered pigpio callbacks for both rising and falling edges on each sensor. When both sensors simultaneously read HIGH for a continuous duration of at least 500 milliseconds, trigger an alert by setting GPIO17 HIGH for 2 seconds, then LOW. Log each seismic event to seismic_events.txt with an ISO-8601-style timestamp, e.g. '2024-01-15 14:30:00 - Seismic event detected!'. Check pigpio initialisation, the log file open, and callback registration for errors. Install SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handlers that close the log file, set the alert pin LOW, and terminate pigpio. The program should run indefinitely until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads an Analog Devices ADXRS290 dual-axis MEMS gyroscope over the hardware SPI0 bus (CE0 on GPIO8, SCLK on GPIO11, MOSI on GPIO10, MISO on GPIO9) using only the pigpio library, not wiringPi. Continuously read the 16-bit two's-complement X-axis angular-rate register (RATE_XL at address 0x02 and RATE_XH at address 0x03), combine the bytes, and convert to degrees per second using the 200 LSB/deg/s sensitivity. For each SPI read, set the MSB (bit 7) of the register address to 1 to indicate a read, transmit the address, and read the data payload, using a 1 MHz SPI clock and mode 0 (CPOL=0, CPHA=0). Timestamp each reading with clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC) and store it in a thread-safe, in-memory circular buffer with a capacity of 100 entries. If the absolute angular velocity exceeds a threshold of 20.0 deg/s, turn on an LED on GPIO17 as a visual warning, turning it off again once the rate drops back below the threshold. Check the return values of all pigpio initialisation and SPI transfer calls, and on SIGINT or SIGTERM exit gracefully with proper resource cleanup: close SPI, turn off the LED, and terminate pigpio.

Accept a single command-line argument: the total fade duration in seconds (integer, 1-3600). Fade each lamp sequentially from full brightness (100% PWM duty cycle) to off (0%) over the specified duration, with each lamp starting its fade only after the previous one completes, using a PWM range of 0-255 at 100 Hz. Validate the user-supplied duration and check every pigpio initialisation call. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM gracefully by turning off all lamps and releasing resources, ensuring proper cleanup on every exit path. Print status messages at startup, during each lamp's fade, and upon completion or termination.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library (not wiringPi, which is deprecated) to toggle a 5V relay on GPIO17 (physical pin 11) using a TTP223 capacitive touch sensor on GPIO4 (physical pin 7), simulating a smart light switch: each touch toggles the relay on or off. The TTP223 outputs logic HIGH when touched; assume an external pull-down resistor, or configure the internal pull-down via pigpio. The relay is active-high, energized when GPIO17 is HIGH. Debounce each touch with a delay of at least 50 ms after detection. Check every pigpio initialisation call and GPIO operation, handling sensor-absent or bus-error conditions gracefully, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling. The program should run indefinitely until terminated by Ctrl+C.

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <signal.h>
#include <pigpio.h>

#define RELAY_PIN 17
#define SENSOR_PIN 4
#define DEBOUNCE_DELAY 50

static volatile int keepRunning = 1;

void intHandler(int dummy) {
    keepRunning = 0;
}

int main(int argc, char *argv[]) {
    if (gpioInitialise() < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to initialize pigpio library\n");
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    gpioSetMode(RELAY_PIN, PI_OUTPUT);
    gpioSetMode(SENSOR_PIN, PI_INPUT);
    gpioSetPullUpDown(SENSOR_PIN, PI_PUD_DOWN);

    signal(SIGINT, intHandler);

    int lastSensorState = 0;
    int relayState = 0;

    while (keepRunning) {
        int sensorState = gpioRead(SENSOR_PIN);

        if (sensorState != lastSensorState) {
            if (sensorState == 1) {
                relayState = !relayState;
                gpioWrite(RELAY_PIN, relayState);
            }

            lastSensorState = sensorState;
            gpioDelay(DEBOUNCE_DELAY * 1000);
        }
    }

    gpioTerminate();
    return EXIT_SUCCESS;
}

If the sensor state has changed, it checks if the sensor is being touched (sensorState == 1) and toggles the relay state accordingly. The relay state is then written to the relay pin using gpioWrite.

The program also includes a debounce delay of 50 ms after each sensor state change to avoid false readings. The lastSensorState variable is updated to the current sensor state and the loop continues.

The program uses the keepRunning variable to control the loop and terminate gracefully when SIGINT is received. The gpioTerminate() function is called to cleanly release the GPIO resources before exiting the program.

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <time.h>
#include <pigpio.h>

#define GPIO_PIN 17
#define VIDEO_DIR "/home/pi/videos/"
#define LOG_FILE "/home/pi/logs/motion_log.txt"
#define VIDEO_DURATION 5
#define DEBOUNCE_DELAY 200

int main(int argc, char *argv[])
{
    int handle, rc;
    char filename[128];
    char command[256];
    time_t now;
    struct tm *timeinfo;

    // Initialize pigpio
    if (gpioInitialise() < 0)
    {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to initialize pigpio\n");
        return 1;
    }

    // Set GPIO pin as input with pull-up
    gpioSetMode(GPIO_PIN, PI_INPUT);
    gpioSetPullUpDown(GPIO_PIN, PI_PUD_UP);

    // Open log file for appending
    FILE *log = fopen(LOG_FILE, "a");
    if (log == NULL)
    {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to open log file\n");
        gpioTerminate();
        return 1;
    }

    // Set up signal handler for SIGINT
    signal(SIGINT, sigintHandler);

    // Set up callback for GPIO pin
    handle = gpioSetAlertFuncEx(GPIO_PIN, motionDetected, NULL);
    if (handle < 0)
    {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to set alert function\n");
        fclose(log);
        gpioTerminate();
        return 1;
    }

    // Main loop
    while (1)
    {
        // Wait for motion detection
        gpioWaitAlert(GPIO_PIN, 0);

        // Debounce
        gpioSleep(PI_TIME_RELATIVE, 0, DEBOUNCE_DELAY * 1000);

        // Record video
        now = time(NULL);
        timeinfo = localtime(&now);
        strftime(filename, sizeof(filename), "%Y%m%d_%H%M%S.h264", timeinfo);
        snprintf(command, sizeof(command), "raspivid -t %d -o %s%s", VIDEO_DURATION * 1000, VIDEO_DIR, filename);
        rc = system(command);
        if (rc != 0)
        {
            fprintf(stderr, "Failed to execute raspivid\n");
        }

        // Log event
        fprintf(log, "%s: Motion detected\n", asctime(timeinfo));
        fflush(log);
    }

    // Clean up
    fclose(log);
    gpioTerminate();
    return 0;
}

void motionDetected(int gpio, int level, uint32_t tick, void *user)
{
    // Ignore spurious triggers
    if (level == PI_TIMEOUT)
        return;

    // Debounce
    gpioSleep(PI_TIME_RELATIVE, 0, DEBOUNCE_DELAY * 1000);

    // Record video
    system("raspivid -t 5000 -o /home/pi/videos/video.h264");
}

void sigintHandler(int signum)
{
    // Close log file
    fclose(log);

    // Terminate pigpio
    gpioTerminate();

    // Exit
    exit(0);
}

This program uses the pigpio library to detect motion with a Keyes KY-033 IR Obstacle Avoidance Sensor on GPIO 17 (physical pin 11). On motion detection, it executes raspivid to record a 5-second video saved to /home/pi/videos/ with a timestamp-based filename such as 20250321_143022.h264, and logs each event with an ISO 8601 timestamp to /home/pi/logs/motion_log.txt. It implements debouncing with a 200 ms minimum interval between triggers.

The program handles errors gracefully by checking pigpio initialization, file operations, and system command execution. It installs a SIGINT signal handler for clean shutdown that closes the log file and terminates pigpio, and keeps the program running continuously until interrupted.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to read X, Y, and Z angular velocities from an MPU-6050 gyroscope over I2C bus 1 at address 0x68 (AD0 pin low), for a basic vibration monitoring system. Initialize the sensor by writing 0x00 to register 0x6B to wake it, 0x07 to register 0x19 to set the sample rate divider to 125 Hz, and 0x00 to register 0x1B to set the gyroscope full-scale range to ±250°/s. Read the raw signed 16-bit gyroscope values from registers 0x43-0x48 (X_H, X_L, Y_H, Y_L, Z_H, Z_L) using a combined I2C block read, and convert them to degrees per second using a sensitivity of 131.0 LSB/(°/s). Sample at 100 Hz (10 ms interval) and log each reading to gyro_log.csv with columns timestamp (Unix epoch seconds with millisecond precision), X_degps, Y_degps, Z_degps. On a read failure, attempt sensor re-initialization (re-wake and re-configure) up to 3 times before logging an error and continuing. Check every pigpio call (gpioInitialise, i2cOpen, i2cWriteByteData, i2cReadI2CBlockData). Use a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler to close the log file and release the I2C handle, and run indefinitely until interrupted.

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <stdint.h>
#include <pigpio.h>
#include <time.h>
#include <signal.h>

#define I2C_ADDR 0x68
#define I2C_BUS 1
#define I2C_FREQ 100000
#define I2C_TIMEOUT 1000
#define I2C_REG_PWR_MGMT_1 0x6B
#define I2C_REG_SMPLRT_DIV 0x19
#define I2C_REG_GYRO_CONFIG 0x1B
#define I2C_REG_GYRO_X_H 0x43
#define I2C_REG_GYRO_X_L 0x44
#define I2C_REG_GYRO_Y_H 0x45
#define I2C_REG_GYRO_Y_L 0x46
#define I2C_REG_GYRO_Z_H 0x47
#define I2C_REG_GYRO_Z_L 0x48
#define I2C_SENSITIVITY 131.0
#define I2C_TIMEOUT_RETRIES 3
#define SAMPLE_INTERVAL_MS 10

FILE *log_file;
int i2c_handle;

void sig_handler(int signo)
{
    if (signo == SIGINT || signo == SIGTERM)
    {
        fclose(log_file);
        gpioTerminate();
        exit(0);
    }
}

int main(int argc, char *argv[])
{
    int i2c_retries;
    int i2c_result;
    uint8_t i2c_buf[14];
    int16_t gyro_x, gyro_y, gyro_z;
    double gyro_x_degps, gyro_y_degps, gyro_z_degps;
    struct timespec ts;
    double timestamp;

    if (gpioInitialise() < 0)
    {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to initialize pigpio library\n");
        return 1;
    }

    signal(SIGINT, sig_handler);
    signal(SIGTERM, sig_handler);

    log_file = fopen("gyro_log.csv", "w");
    if (log_file == NULL)
    {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to open log file\n");
        gpioTerminate();
        return 1;
    }

    i2c_handle = i2cOpen(I2C_BUS, I2C_ADDR, I2C_FREQ);
    if (i2c_handle < 0)
    {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to open I2C bus\n");
        fclose(log_file);
        gpioTerminate();
        return 1;
    }

    i2c_retries = 0;
    while (i2c_retries < I2C_TIMEOUT_RETRIES)
    {
        i2c_result = i2cWriteByteData(i2c_handle, I2C_REG_PWR_MGMT_1, 0x00);
        if (i2c_result < 0)
        {
            fprintf(stderr, "Failed to write to I2C register\n");
            i2c_retries++;
            continue;
        }

        i2c_result = i2cWriteByteData(i2c_handle, I2C_REG_SMPLRT_DIV, 0x07);
        if (i2c_result < 0)
        {
            fprintf(stderr, "Failed to write to I2C register\n");
            i2c_retries++;
            continue;
        }

        i2c_result = i2cWriteByteData(i2c_handle, I2C_REG_GYRO_CONFIG, 0x00);
        if (i2c_result < 0)
        {
            fprintf(stderr, "Failed to write to I2C register\n");
            i2c_retries++;
            continue;
        }

        break;
    }

    if (i2c_retries == I2C_TIMEOUT_RETRIES)
    {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to initialize sensor\n");
        fclose(log_file);
        i2cClose(i2c_handle);
        gpioTerminate();
        return 1;
    }

    fprintf(log_file, "timestamp,X_degps,Y_degps,Z_degps\n");

    while (1)
    {
        i2c_result = i2cReadI2CBlockData(i2c_handle, I2C_REG_GYRO_X_H, 14, i2c_buf);
        if (i2c_result < 0)
        {
            fprintf(stderr, "Failed to read from I2C register\n");

            {
                i2c_result = i2cWriteByteData(i2c_handle, I2C_REG_PWR_MGMT_1, 0x00);
                if (i2c_result < 0)
                {
                    fprintf(stderr, "Failed to write to I2C register\n");
                    i2c_retries++;
                    continue;
                }

                i2c_result = i2cWriteByteData(i2c_handle, I2C_REG_SMPLRT_DIV, 0x07);
                if (i2c_result < 0)
                {
                    fprintf(stderr, "Failed to write to I2C register\n");
                    i2c_retries++;
                    continue;
                }

                i2c_result = i2cWriteByteData(i2c_handle, I2C_REG_GYRO_CONFIG, 0x00);
                if (i2c_result < 0)
                {
                    fprintf(stderr, "Failed to write to I2C register\n");
                    i2c_retries++;
                    continue;
                }

                break;
            }

            if (i2c_retries == I2C_TIMEOUT_RETRIES)
            {
                fprintf(stderr, "Failed to re-initialize sensor\n");
                fclose(log_file);
                i2cClose(i2c_handle);
                gpioTerminate();
                return 1;
            }

            continue;
        }

        gyro_x = (i2c_buf[0] << 8) | i2c_buf[1];
        gyro_y = (i2c_buf[2] << 8) | i2c_buf[3];
        gyro_z = (i2c_buf[4] << 8) | i2c_buf[5];

        gyro_x_degps = gyro_x / I2C_SENSITIVITY;
        gyro_y_degps = gyro_y / I2C_SENSITIVITY;
        gyro_z_degps = gyro_z / I2C_SENSITIVITY;

        clock_gettime(CLOCK_REALTIME, &ts);
        timestamp = ts.tv_sec + (ts.tv_nsec / 1000000000.0);

        fprintf(log_file, "%f,%f,%f,%f\n", timestamp, gyro_x_degps, gyro_y_degps, gyro_z_degps);

        gpioDelay(SAMPLE_INTERVAL_MS * 1000);
    }

    fclose(log_file);
    i2cClose(i2c_handle);
    gpioTerminate();

    return 0;
}
```

### Explanation:
The program uses the pigpio library to read X, Y, and Z angular velocities from an MPU-6050 gyroscope over I2C bus 1 at address 0x68 (AD0 pin low). It initializes the sensor by writing 0x00 to register 0x6B to wake it, 0x07 to register 0x19 to set the sample rate divider to 125 Hz, and 0x00 to register 0x1B to set the gyroscope full-scale range to ±250°/s. It reads the raw signed 16-bit gyroscope values from registers 0x43-0x48 (X_H, X_L, Y_H, Y_L, Z_H, Z_L) using a combined I2C block read, and converts them to degrees per second using a sensitivity of 131.0 LSB/(°/s). It samples at 100 Hz (10 ms interval) and logs each reading to gyro_log.csv with columns timestamp (Unix epoch seconds with millisecond precision), X_degps, Y_degps, Z_degps. On a read failure, it attempts sensor re-initialization (re-wake and re-configure) up to 3 times before logging an error and continuing. It checks every pigpio call (gpioInitialise, i2cOpen, i2cWriteByteData, i2cReadI2CBlockData). It uses a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler to close the log file and release the I2C handle, and runs indefinitely until interrupted.

On a confirmed freefall, drive GPIO27 high to simulate an alarm, hold it for 5 seconds, then set it low. Log each freefall event to freefall.log in CSV format with a timestamp (YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS) and x, y, z values to 3 decimal places. Handle I2C errors by printing to stderr and continuing operation, checking every pigpio and I2C call. Use a SIGINT handler to close the I2C handle, set GPIO low, and terminate pigpio.

Log each valid distance measurement in centimeters with a nanosecond-precision timestamp to distance_log.txt in CSV format: timestamp_ns,distance_cm. Protect the shared pulse-timing variables, which are updated from interrupt context, with a mutex. Handle pigpio initialization failure, file open failure, invalid pulse widths, and sensor timeouts. Write a C program that uses the pigpio library to control a door-lock servo on a Raspberry Pi. The servo is connected to GPIO 18 (physical pin 12, BCM 18). Two momentary push-buttons are wired to GPIO 21 (BCM) and GPIO 22 (BCM), each connecting its pin to ground when pressed, so internal pull-ups must be enabled. Pressing the GPIO 21 button drives the servo to the locked position with a 2000 µs pulse width; pressing the GPIO 22 button drives it to the unlocked position with a 1000 µs pulse width. Check the return value of gpioInitialise() and exit with an error message on failure, and verify that gpioServo() succeeds for both pulse-width commands. Implement button debouncing so a single press is not registered multiple times, waiting for release plus a short debounce delay, and poll the buttons in a tight loop with a small sleep to avoid high CPU usage. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler so Ctrl+C cleanly stops the servo (pulse width 0) and calls gpioTerminate() before exiting. Print status messages to stdout for lock, unlock, and shutdown events.
raw:
```
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <signal.h>
#include <pigpio.h>

#define SERVO_PIN 18
#define LOCK_BUTTON_PIN 21
#define UNLOCK_BUTTON_PIN 22
#define LOCK_PULSE_WIDTH 2000
#define UNLOCK_PULSE_WIDTH 1000
#define DEBOUNCE_DELAY 100000

static volatile int keepRunning = 1;

void intHandler(int dummy) {
    keepRunning = 0;
}

int main(int argc, char *argv[]) {
    if (gpioInitialise() < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to initialize GPIO\n");
        return 1;
    }

    gpioSetMode(SERVO_PIN, PI_OUTPUT);
    gpioSetMode(LOCK_BUTTON_PIN, PI_INPUT);
    gpioSetMode(UNLOCK_BUTTON_PIN, PI_INPUT);
    gpioSetPullUpDown(LOCK_BUTTON_PIN, PI_PUD_UP);
    gpioSetPullUpDown(UNLOCK_BUTTON_PIN, PI_PUD_UP);

    signal(SIGINT, intHandler);
    signal(SIGTERM, intHandler);

    int lastLockButtonState = 1;
    int lastUnlockButtonState = 1;
    int lockButtonState;
    int unlockButtonState;
    int lockServo = 0;
    int unlockServo = 0;

    while (keepRunning) {
        lockButtonState = gpioRead(LOCK_BUTTON_PIN);
        unlockButtonState = gpioRead(UNLOCK_BUTTON_PIN);

        if (lockButtonState != lastLockButtonState) {
            if (lockButtonState == 0) {
                lockServo = 1;
            }
            lastLockButtonState = lockButtonState;
        }

        if (unlockButtonState != lastUnlockButtonState) {
            if (unlockButtonState == 0) {
                unlockServo = 1;
            }
            lastUnlockButtonState = unlockButtonState;
        }

        if (lockServo) {
            gpioServo(SERVO_PIN, LOCK_PULSE_WIDTH);
            printf("Locked\n");
            lockServo = 0;
        }

        if (unlockServo) {
            gpioServo(SERVO_PIN, UNLOCK_PULSE_WIDTH);
            printf("Unlocked\n");
            unlockServo = 0;
        }

        gpioDelay(DEBOUNCE_DELAY);
    }

    gpioServo(SERVO_PIN, 0);
    gpioTerminate();

    return 0;
}

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to implement a smart security light. Monitor a PIR motion sensor on GPIO 4 (physical pin 7, input). On a rising edge (motion detected), activate a relay-controlled 12V LED floodlight on GPIO 17 (physical pin 11, output) for exactly 60 seconds, then turn it off. Log every activation event with an ISO-8601 timestamp and every deactivation event with timestamp and measured duration in seconds to security_log.txt in append mode. Check pigpio initialization, every gpioSetMode/gpioWrite/gpioRead return code, and every fopen/fprintf/fclose result; on a file error, turn off the floodlight before exiting. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler so Ctrl+C cleanly turns off the floodlight, releases pigpio resources, and exits with code 0. Poll at a 100 ms interval to avoid busy-waiting, and ensure the floodlight is off on every exit path. Do not use wiringPi.

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <pigpio.h>
#include <time.h>

#define TOUCH_SENSOR_PIN 4
#define RELAY_PIN 17

int main(void)
{
    int touchSensorState = 0;
    int relayState = 0;
    int lastTouchSensorState = 0;
    int lastRelayState = 0;
    int rc = 0;
    int gpio = 0;
    time_t timestamp;
    struct tm *timeInfo;
    char timeString[20];

    // Initialize pigpio
    if ((gpio = gpioInitialise()) < 0)
    {
        fprintf(stderr, "pigpio initialisation failed: %d\n", gpio);
        return 1;
    }

    // Set GPIO 4 as input
    if (gpioSetMode(gpio, TOUCH_SENSOR_PIN, PI_INPUT) != 0)
    {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to set GPIO 4 as input\n");
        gpioTerminate();
        return 1;
    }

    // Set GPIO 17 as output
    if (gpioSetMode(gpio, RELAY_PIN, PI_OUTPUT) != 0)
    {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to set GPIO 17 as output\n");
        gpioTerminate();
        return 1;
    }

    // Set initial relay state
    if (gpioWrite(gpio, RELAY_PIN, relayState) != 0)
    {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to set initial relay state\n");
        gpioTerminate();
        return 1;
    }

    // Main loop
    while (1)
    {
        // Read touch sensor state
        touchSensorState = gpioRead(gpio, TOUCH_SENSOR_PIN);

        // Check for edge
        if (touchSensorState != lastTouchSensorState)
        {
            // Debounce
            time_t startTime = time(NULL);
            do
            {
                touchSensorState = gpioRead(gpio, TOUCH_SENSOR_PIN);
            } while (touchSensorState != lastTouchSensorState && difftime(time(NULL), startTime) < 0.05);

            // Toggle relay state
            if (touchSensorState == lastTouchSensorState)
            {
                relayState = !relayState;
                if (gpioWrite(gpio, RELAY_PIN, relayState) != 0)
                {
                    fprintf(stderr, "Failed to toggle relay state\n");
                    gpioTerminate();
                    return 1;
                }

                // Log state change
                timestamp = time(NULL);
                timeInfo = localtime(&timestamp);
                strftime(timeString, sizeof(timeString), "%FT%T%z", timeInfo);
                printf("%s: Relay state changed to %s\n", timeString, relayState ? "ON" : "OFF");
            }
        }

        // Update last states
        lastTouchSensorState = touchSensorState;
        lastRelayState = relayState;

        // Sleep for 10 ms
        gpioDelay(10000);
    }

    // Graceful shutdown
    if (gpioWrite(gpio, RELAY_PIN, 0) != 0)
    {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to turn relay OFF\n");
        gpioTerminate();
        return 1;
    }

    gpioTerminate();
    printf("Exiting...\n");

    return 0;
}

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the pigpio library to read flow rate from a YF-S201 water flow sensor on GPIO 17 (physical pin 11), computing liters per minute (LPM) from its 450 pulses-per-liter calibration as LPM = (pulses / 450.0) * 60.0. Trigger a solenoid valve on GPIO 27 to shut off when the rate exceeds 5.0 L/min, reopening only when it drops below 4.5 L/min (0.5 L/min hysteresis); the solenoid is open (HIGH) by default and closes (LOW) above the threshold. Initialize pigpio and validate all return codes (gpioInitialise, gpioSetMode, gpioWrite, gpioSetISRFuncEx), using a 1-second ISR debounce timeout on the flow sensor pin. Protect the shared pulse counter with a pthread mutex; sample the pulse count every 1 second and reset it after computing LPM. Log every LPM reading and every solenoid state change with timestamps to water_flow.log; if the log file cannot be opened, clean up all initialized resources and exit with a non-zero status. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM by logging the event, reopening the solenoid to its safe state, closing the log file, destroying the mutex, and calling gpioTerminate.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the pigpio library, not bcm2835 or wiringPi, to read data from an HX711 load cell amplifier connected to GPIO 23 (DATA) and GPIO 24 (SCK), calibrate the readings using a known weight, and control an SG90-style servo motor on GPIO 18 via hardware PWM to dispense a pre-determined amount of ingredient based on the weight. The program must act as a TCP server listening on 127.0.0.1:12345: receive a target weight in grams from a client, open the servo to dispense, wait 1 second for the load cell to stabilize, read the actual weight from the HX711, send the actual weight back to the client, and log each dispensing event (date, time, target weight, actual weight, and any error message) as a JSON object appended to dispensing_log.json. Implement robust error handling for pigpio initialization, HX711 communication timeouts (sensor absent or not ready), servo control failures, file I/O, and network errors. Use signal handlers (SIGINT, SIGTERM) for clean shutdown of GPIO, sockets, and the servo. Read calibration_factor, server_ip, and server_port from a config.ini file, falling back to defaults if the file is missing or malformed. Read the HX711 using bit-banged GPIO with a 1 µs clock pulse width, timing out if DATA stays HIGH for more than 1000 attempts. Map the target weight to the servo's 1000-2000 µs pulse-width range.

On each valid rising edge (LOW to HIGH), toggle the relay. Log every relay state change to the console with a timestamp in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS Relay: ON' or '... Relay: OFF'. Install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers for graceful shutdown: turn the relay OFF, release pigpio resources, and exit cleanly. Keep the program self-contained, with no networking, Redis, or ZeroMQ code.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 or 5 (40-pin header) that uses the pigpio library, not WiringPi or direct /dev/mem register access, to control a standard hobby servo such as an SG90 connected to GPIO18 (physical pin 12) via hardware PWM. The user increments or decrements the servo angle via keyboard input without pressing Enter (raw terminal mode): '+' increases the angle by 10°, '-' decreases it by 10°, and 'q' quits, with the angle clamped to 0-180°. Use 50 Hz PWM (20 ms period) with a pulse width of 500-2500 µs spanning 0-180°, starting at 90° (1500 µs), and drive it with gpioServo() rather than raw register writes. Check the return value of gpioInitialise(), printing to stderr and exiting non-zero on failure, and validate that computed pulse widths stay within [500, 2500] µs. On 'q' or SIGINT (Ctrl-C), stop PWM pulses on GPIO18, call gpioTerminate(), and restore the terminal settings, saving and restoring termios even on an unexpected exit. Print the current angle after each change.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the modern libgpiod API, not wiringPi, to monitor a conveyor-belt motor using an A3144 Hall-effect sensor on GPIO 17 (physical pin 11, BCM). A two-pole magnet on the motor shaft produces one pulse per revolution, detected on the rising edge. Configure GPIO 17 as input with the internal pull-up enabled via the GPIOD_LINE_REQUEST_FLAG_BIAS_PULL_UP bias flag, since the A3144's open-collector output requires a pull-up. Use edge-triggered event detection (gpiod_line_event_wait) to count pulses, with a 2 ms debounce window to reject contact bounce and double-edge noise. Every 5 seconds, compute RPM = (pulseCount / 5.0) * 60.0, append the sample to motor_rpm.log in CSV format (timestamp in ISO 8601, rpm_value to 2 decimal places), flushing after every write, and print the current RPM to stdout. Check the return values of gpiod_chip_open, gpiod_chip_get_line, and gpiod_line_request_input_flags, printing clear diagnostics to stderr and exiting non-zero on failure. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown: stop the main loop, release the GPIO line, close the chip, close the log file, and exit cleanly. Use the monotonic clock (clock_gettime with CLOCK_MONOTONIC) for timing, not clock().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the pigpio library to control a 5V relay on GPIO17 based on a TTP223 capacitive touch sensor on GPIO4, which outputs 3.3V logic HIGH when touched and LOW otherwise; the relay module is active-HIGH. On the rising edge of a touch, toggle the relay state, polling the sensor every 50 ms. Implement a failsafe: if the touch sensor remains continuously HIGH for more than 10 seconds, force the relay OFF and ignore further toggles until the sensor is released. Check the return value of gpioInitialise() and every gpioSetMode()/gpioWrite()/gpioRead() call; if gpioRead() returns PI_BAD_GPIO, log the error and exit. Install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that set a volatile flag so the main loop can exit cleanly; perform the actual cleanup — releasing the relay (set OFF) and calling gpioTerminate() — in main() after the loop exits, not inside the signal handler itself.

Drive the valve via PWM on GPIO 18 (BCM, hardware PWM 0), with enable/direction control on GPIO 23 (BCM), active-high, and count pulses from a YF-S201 flow sensor on GPIO 24 (BCM) via an interrupt-driven, rising-edge pulse counter. Accept the target flow rate in L/min as a command-line argument (-t, e.g. -t 5.0), validating it and exiting with an error message if missing or invalid. Sample the flow rate every 100 ms, computing L/min from the pulse count accumulated over the interval using the YF-S201 calibration of 450 pulses per liter, and use a proportional controller (Kp = 1.0) to adjust the valve PWM duty cycle (0-255), clamped to [0, 255], to maintain the target flow rate. Log timestamp_ms, flow_rate, and valve_position to flow_log.csv on every control iteration, logging only to this local file with no UDP or network logging. Enable the valve (GPIO 23 high) at startup; on shutdown, set PWM to 0, drive GPIO 23 low, close the log file, and cleanly terminate pigpio. Check pigpio initialization, GPIO mode setup, ISR registration, and file open, exiting with a diagnostic on any failure, and handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown and resource release.

#include <pigpio.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <time.h>

#define MOTOR_1 17
#define MOTOR_2 27
#define MIN_DUTY_CYCLE 0
#define MAX_DUTY_CYCLE 255
#define MIN_DURATION 50
#define MAX_DURATION 200
#define MIN_STEPS 5
#define MAX_STEPS 15

int main(void)
{
    if (gpioInitialise() < 0)
    {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to initialize pigpio library\n");
        return 1;
    }

    gpioSetMode(MOTOR_1, PI_OUTPUT);
    gpioSetMode(MOTOR_2, PI_OUTPUT);

    srand(time(NULL));

    while (1)
    {
        int num_steps = rand() % (MAX_STEPS - MIN_STEPS + 1) + MIN_STEPS;

        for (int i = 0; i < num_steps; i++)
        {
            int duty_cycle_1 = rand() % (MAX_DUTY_CYCLE - MIN_DUTY_CYCLE + 1) + MIN_DUTY_CYCLE;
            int duty_cycle_2 = rand() % (MAX_DUTY_CYCLE - MIN_DUTY_CYCLE + 1) + MIN_DUTY_CYCLE;
            int duration = rand() % (MAX_DURATION - MIN_DURATION + 1) + MIN_DURATION;

            gpioPWM(MOTOR_1, duty_cycle_1);
            gpioPWM(MOTOR_2, duty_cycle_2);
            gpioDelay(duration);
        }
    }

    gpioTerminate();

    return 0;
}

Use only libgpiod APIs — gpiod_chip_open_by_name, gpiod_chip_get_line, gpiod_line_request_bulk_inputs/outputs, gpiod_line_get_value, gpiod_line_set_value, gpiod_line_release, and gpiod_chip_close. #include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <time.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <errno.h>
#include <signal.h>
#include <gpiod.h>

#define SENSOR_GPIO 16
#define RELAY_GPIO 20
#define LOG_FILE "relay_events.log"

static struct gpiod_chip *chip;
static struct gpiod_line *sensor_line, *relay_line;
static FILE *log_file;

static void cleanup(void)
{
    if (sensor_line)
        gpiod_line_release(sensor_line);
    if (relay_line)
        gpiod_line_release(relay_line);
    if (chip)
        gpiod_chip_close(chip);
    if (log_file)
        fclose(log_file);
}

static void sig_handler(int signum)
{
    cleanup();
    exit(EXIT_SUCCESS);
}

int main(void)
{
    int sensor_value, relay_value = 0;
    struct timespec ts;
    char timestamp[32];

    if (signal(SIGINT, sig_handler) == SIG_ERR ||
        signal(SIGTERM, sig_handler) == SIG_ERR) {
        perror("signal");
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    chip = gpiod_chip_open_by_name("gpiochip0");
    if (!chip) {
        perror("gpiod_chip_open_by_name");
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    sensor_line = gpiod_chip_get_line(chip, SENSOR_GPIO);
    if (!sensor_line) {
        perror("gpiod_chip_get_line");
        goto error;
    }

    if (gpiod_line_request_input(sensor_line, "sensor") < 0) {
        perror("gpiod_line_request_input");
        goto error;
    }

    relay_line = gpiod_chip_get_line(chip, RELAY_GPIO);
    if (!relay_line) {
        perror("gpiod_chip_get_line");
        goto error;
    }

    if (gpiod_line_request_output(relay_line, "relay", 0) < 0) {
        perror("gpiod_line_request_output");
        goto error;
    }

    log_file = fopen(LOG_FILE, "a");
    if (!log_file) {
        perror("fopen");
        goto error;
    }

    while (1) {
        sensor_value = gpiod_line_get_value(sensor_line);
        if (sensor_value < 0) {
            perror("gpiod_line_get_value");
            goto error;
        }

        if (sensor_value != relay_value) {
            relay_value = !relay_value;
            if (gpiod_line_set_value(relay_line, relay_value) < 0) {
                perror("gpiod_line_set_value");
                goto error;
            }

            clock_gettime(CLOCK_REALTIME, &ts);
            strftime(timestamp, sizeof(timestamp), "%FT%T%z",
                     gmtime(&ts.tv_sec));
            fprintf(log_file, "%s: relay %s\n", timestamp,
                    relay_value ? "on" : "off");
            fflush(log_file);
        }

        usleep(100000);
    }

error:
    cleanup();
    return EXIT_FAILURE;
}

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads ambient light levels from four BH1750FVI sensors on the I2C-1 bus at 7-bit addresses 0x23, 0x24, 0x25, and 0x26, using the standard Linux I2C ioctl interface (<linux/i2c-dev.h> with open() and ioctl(I2C_SLAVE)) rather than wiringPi. Note that the BH1750 natively supports only addresses 0x23 and 0x5C via its ADDR pin, so addresses 0x24-0x26 require an I2C multiplexer or level-shifted address lines; assume the hardware is wired accordingly. For each sensor, open /dev/i2c-1 (a single shared file descriptor or one per sensor is acceptable), set the slave address with ioctl(I2C_SLAVE, addr) before each transaction, write the One-Time High-Resolution mode command byte 0x20, wait 180 ms for conversion, then read 2 bytes. Convert the big-endian result to lux using lux = ((data[0] << 8) | data[1]) / 1.2. Once per second, broadcast all four readings as a single UDP multicast packet to 239.255.255.250:5005, formatted as semicolon-separated sensor_id,lux pairs, e.g. 1,120.5;2,85.0;3,210.5;4,45.0. If any sensor fails — open error, address-set error, write error, read error, or partial read — report NaN for that sensor and continue. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM by setting a flag to exit the loop cleanly, and close all file descriptors, both I2C and UDP socket, on every exit path.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads airflow data from a Honeywell AWM7300V mass airflow sensor at I2C address 0x28 on /dev/i2c-1, using the Linux I2C character device interface (<linux/i2c-dev.h>, <sys/ioctl.h>, read() and write() syscalls) rather than wiringPi. To read flow data, issue a zero-length I2C write as a start condition followed by a 2-byte read; the sensor returns a 14-bit flow value in the first two bytes, masked with 0x3FFF. Convert the raw value to SLPM using flow = (raw - 3277) * 0.1, sampling once per second, and log each timestamped flow rate to airflow_log.txt. Check every syscall, retry transient I2C read failures up to 3 times with 100 ms delays between retries, and handle sensor-absent (ENXIO) and bus-error (EIO) conditions. Install a SIGINT handler that closes the I2C file descriptor and flushes the log file for a clean shutdown.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that interfaces with an Adafruit AS7341 10-Channel Light/Color Sensor over I2C using the Linux i2c-dev kernel interface — opening /dev/i2c-1 and using ioctl with I2C_SLAVE to set the 7-bit address 0x39 — rather than wiringPi. Perform a proper initialization sequence: verify the WHO_AM_I/ID register at 0x24 equals 0x19, power the sensor on via the PON bit in the ENABLE register at 0x80, configure SMUX for spectral readings via the CFG6 register at 0xAF, and enable spectral measurement via the SP_EN bit. Read all 10 spectral channels — F1 through F8, Clear, and NIR — from their registers at 0x60-0x73, compute a simplified lux approximation, and log the results with a timestamp to spectral_log.csv every 5 seconds in comma-separated format. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that interfaces with an Omron D7S seismic sensor over I2C using the Linux i2c-dev kernel interface (opening /dev/i2c-1 and using ioctl I2C_SLAVE) rather than wiringPi. Read the 6 bytes of tri-axial acceleration starting at register 0x28 — X_L, X_H, Y_L, Y_H, Z_L, Z_H, little-endian signed 16-bit — and convert to g using g = raw * 0.000244 for the ±8 g range. Continuously read the asynchronous TLV byte stream, synchronize on the 8-byte magic word 0x0204 0x0306 0x0805 0x0709 (little-endian), validate the TLV payload, and extract each detected object's range and velocity. For each detected object, write a row to radar_data.csv with columns timestamp, object_index, range_m, velocity_mps. Check every UART read, handle partial reads and buffer overflows gracefully, skip malformed frames, and log errors to stderr without crashing. On all exit paths, including SIGINT and SIGTERM, close the UART, flush and close the CSV file, and call gpioTerminate().

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library, not wiringPi, to read a Keywish 3-Way Tracking Sensor (KY-033) with its left, middle, and right IR emitter/detector outputs connected to GPIO4 (pin 7), GPIO17 (pin 11), and GPIO27 (pin 13) respectively, each configured as an input with pull-up resistors enabled; the sensor's 5V and GND are wired to the Pi's 5V and GND pins. Each output reads digital LOW when an obstacle or line is detected and HIGH when clear. If pigpio initialization fails, print an error and exit with code 1; if a gpioRead call fails, print an error and continue rather than exiting. Running the main loop at 10 Hz (a 100 ms period), read all three sensors each cycle and log their states to the console with a timestamp, using 0 for obstacle detected and 1 for clear. If all three sensors read 0 simultaneously, send the string \"EMERGENCY STOP!\\n\" over the serial port /dev/ttyAMA0 at 115200 baud, 8N1, with no flow control, handling any serial write error by printing it and continuing rather than exiting. Register SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers to close the serial port and terminate pigpio before exit, and release all resources on any error path.
raw:
```c
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <pigpio.h>
#include <time.h>
#include <signal.h>
#include <unistd.h>

#define LEFT_SENSOR 4
#define MIDDLE_SENSOR 17
#define RIGHT_SENSOR 27
#define BAUD_RATE 115200
#define SERIAL_PORT "/dev/ttyAMA0"

int left_sensor_state = 0;
int middle_sensor_state = 0;
int right_sensor_state = 0;

int serial_handle = -1;

void sig_handler(int signo)
{
    if (signo == SIGINT || signo == SIGTERM)
    {
        if (serial_handle != -1)
        {
            gpioSerWrite(serial_handle, "EMERGENCY STOP!\n");
            gpioSerClose(serial_handle);
        }
        gpioTerminate();
        exit(0);
    }
}

int main(int argc, char *argv[])
{
    if (gpioInitialise() < 0)
    {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to initialize pigpio library\n");
        return 1;
    }

    signal(SIGINT, sig_handler);
    signal(SIGTERM, sig_handler);

    serial_handle = gpioSerOpen(SERIAL_PORT, BAUD_RATE, 0);
    if (serial_handle < 0)
    {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to open serial port %s\n", SERIAL_PORT);
        return 1;
    }

    gpioSetMode(LEFT_SENSOR, PI_INPUT);
    gpioSetPullUpDown(LEFT_SENSOR, PI_PUD_UP);

    gpioSetMode(MIDDLE_SENSOR, PI_INPUT);
    gpioSetPullUpDown(MIDDLE_SENSOR, PI_PUD_UP);

    gpioSetMode(RIGHT_SENSOR, PI_INPUT);
    gpioSetPullUpDown(RIGHT_SENSOR, PI_PUD_UP);

    struct timespec start_time, current_time;
    clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC, &start_time);

    while (1)
    {
        clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC, &current_time);
        if (current_time.tv_sec - start_time.tv_sec >= 10)
        {
            start_time = current_time;

            left_sensor_state = gpioRead(LEFT_SENSOR);
            if (left_sensor_state < 0)
            {
                fprintf(stderr, "Failed to read left sensor\n");
                continue;
            }

            middle_sensor_state = gpioRead(MIDDLE_SENSOR);
            if (middle_sensor_state < 0)
            {
                fprintf(stderr, "Failed to read middle sensor\n");
                continue;
            }

            right_sensor_state = gpioRead(RIGHT_SENSOR);
            if (right_sensor_state < 0)
            {
                fprintf(stderr, "Failed to read right sensor\n");
                continue;
            }

            printf("%ld.%09ld, %d, %d, %d\n", current_time.tv_sec, current_time.tv_nsec, left_sensor_state, middle_sensor_state, right_sensor_state);

            if (left_sensor_state == 0 && middle_sensor_state == 0 && right_sensor_state == 0)
            {
                gpioSerWrite(serial_handle, "EMERGENCY STOP!\n");
            }
        }
    }

    return 0;
}
